sources.title: Zoloft · Prescribing information and Medication Guide
sources.note: Current SPL version 7, effective August 8, 2023, published July 24, 2025; prescribing information revised August 2023. Tablets and alcohol-containing oral concentrate.

assertions: In adults, Zoloft is labeled for major depressive disorder (MDD), obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), panic disorder, posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), social anxiety disorder, and premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD).

For children and adolescents aged 6–17 years, OCD is the established labeled indication. Pediatric depression and other pediatric indications are not established in this label. This profile does not provide an exhaustive off-label prescribing guide.

sourceAudit.card: Tablets or equivalent oral dose · Starting regimens
assertions: For inadequate response, increase by 25–50 mg daily no more often than once weekly according to tolerability, up to 200 mg daily. Tablets may be taken with or without food. The concentrate requires dilution.
Adult MDD or OCD: Start 50 mg daily; therapeutic range 50–200 mg daily.
Adult panic disorder, PTSD, social anxiety disorder: Start 25 mg daily; therapeutic range 50–200 mg daily.
OCD · age 6–12 years: Start 25 mg daily; therapeutic range 50–200 mg daily.
OCD · age 13–17 years: Start 50 mg daily; therapeutic range 50–200 mg daily.
Start 50 mg daily in adult women. Continuous treatment: increase in 50 mg increments per menstrual cycle if needed, to a maximum 150 mg daily.

Intermittent treatment: dose during the luteal phase, starting 14 days before anticipated menstruation and continuing through the onset of menses. If 50 mg is inadequate, the next cycle may use 50 mg daily for the first 3 dosing days, then 100 mg daily for the remaining dosing days; maximum 100 mg daily.

Mild hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh 5–6): use half the usual starting dose and half the therapeutic range. Use is not recommended in moderate or severe hepatic impairment. No dose adjustment is needed for mild to severe renal impairment.

Dilute before use. Measure with the supplied calibrated dropper (marked only at 25 mg and 50 mg); confirm an appropriate measuring plan for other prescribed doses. Mix the dose with 4 ounces (½ cup) of water, ginger ale, lemon/lime soda, lemonade, or orange juice only. Take immediately; do not premix. Slight haze after dilution is normal.

The concentrate contains 12% alcohol and is contraindicated with disulfiram. The dropper contains dry natural rubber; review latex sensitivity. Directions do not apply automatically to other sertraline liquids or capsule products.

Screen for personal or family history of bipolar disorder before starting. Allow at least 14 days after stopping an MAOI antidepressant before starting sertraline, and at least 14 days after stopping sertraline before starting an MAOI antidepressant.
Reduce gradually when stopping whenever possible. The taper depends on clinical response and withdrawal symptoms; do not abruptly stop on your own.

Serotonin syndrome can occur alone or with other serotonergic medicines: agitation, fever, sweating, rapid pulse, rigidity, overactive reflexes, tremor, or gastrointestinal symptoms require urgent assessment. Stop sertraline and concomitant serotonergic agents and provide supportive care when the syndrome occurs.

Bleeding risk rises with aspirin, NSAIDs, antiplatelet agents, or anticoagulants. Screen for bipolar disorder because mania or hypomania may emerge. Use cautiously with seizure disorders or QTc-prolongation risk; avoid use in untreated anatomically narrow angles.

Hyponatremia, sometimes related to SIADH, can cause confusion, weakness, unsteadiness, or seizures. Older adults, diuretic users, and volume-depleted patients are at greater risk. Symptomatic hyponatremia requires discontinuation and appropriate treatment.

Abrupt stopping can cause discontinuation symptoms. Ask about sexual function before and during treatment; decreased libido, orgasm difficulties, erectile dysfunction, or delayed ejaculation may occur.

Concomitant MAOIs, including linezolid or intravenous methylene blue, or use within the MAOI washout interval; pimozide; and known sertraline hypersensitivity. Observe the 14-day separation for MAOI antidepressant switches.
Disulfiram is additionally contraindicated with the alcohol-containing Zoloft oral concentrate; this formulation-specific restriction is not a tablet alcohol-content claim.

sourceAudit.card: Boxed warning · Suicidal thoughts and behaviors
assertions: Antidepressants increased suicidal thoughts and behavior in pediatric and young adult patients in short-term trials. Closely monitor all patients for worsening illness or emerging suicidality, particularly in the first months and during dose changes. Educate caregivers to report concerning behavior promptly; emergency danger requires emergency care.

Common trial events included nausea, diarrhea, tremor, indigestion, decreased appetite, sweating, ejaculation failure, and reduced libido. Sleep disturbance, fatigue, or agitation can also occur. Trial rates cannot be used as direct comparisons with other antidepressants.
Serious reported reactions include serotonin syndrome, major bleeding, severe hyponatremia, arrhythmias, hypersensitivity, and severe skin or liver events. Postmarketing frequencies are uncertain.
Highly protein-bound drugs may require monitoring and dose adjustment for adverse effects. Oral concentrate plus disulfiram is contraindicated because of alcohol.
MAOIs; pimozide: Contraindicated. Follow MAOI switch intervals and urgent-treatment instructions.

Other serotonergic drugs: Monitor for serotonin syndrome, particularly at initiation and dose increases; includes other antidepressants, triptans, several opioids, lithium, buspirone, amphetamines, and St. John’s wort.
NSAIDs, aspirin, antiplatelets, anticoagulants: Increased bleeding risk; monitor INR carefully with warfarin.
CYP2D6 substrates: Exposure may rise; adjust substrates if needed (examples include metoprolol, flecainide, atomoxetine). Reassess when sertraline is stopped.
Phenytoin / fosphenytoin: Check phenytoin concentrations at initiation or titration; reduce dose if needed.
Other QT-prolonging medicines: Avoid concomitant use with known QT-prolonging drugs; assess cardiac risk.
Benzodiazepine urine immunoassays may be falsely positive during treatment and for several days after stopping. Confirmatory testing can distinguish sertraline from benzodiazepines.

Consider relapse and untreated-illness risks alongside treatment risks. Overall epidemiologic data do not show a difference in major birth-defect risk with first-trimester sertraline compared with comparator background rates; individual defect findings are inconclusive.

Late-pregnancy SSRI exposure can be associated with neonatal adaptation or discontinuation symptoms and persistent pulmonary hypertension; monitor exposed newborns. Use close to delivery may increase postpartum hemorrhage risk. The 12%-alcohol Zoloft concentrate is not recommended during pregnancy; review a suitable formulation with the clinician. The label lists an antidepressant pregnancy registry.

Published data show low sertraline and metabolite levels in human milk. Effects on milk production are unknown. Consider breastfeeding benefits, maternal treatment need, and possible infant effects together.
Pediatric approval is for OCD at ages 6–17 only. Monitor growth, weight, appetite, behavior, and suicidality during pediatric treatment.
Older adults warrant conservative dose selection and particular attention to hyponatremia, organ function, and interacting medicines.
Enhances central serotonergic activity by inhibiting neuronal serotonin reuptake. It also inhibits serotonin uptake by platelets, relevant to bleeding risk. It does not inhibit monoamine oxidase.
Absorption: Peak plasma concentration about 4.5–8.4 hours after repeated oral dosing.
Half-life / steady state: Parent drug about 26 hours; steady state after about 1 week.
Metabolism: Extensive hepatic first-pass metabolism; N-desmethylsertraline is substantially less active.
Protein binding / elimination: About 98% protein bound; radiolabeled metabolites recovered in urine and feces, with negligible unchanged urinary drug.
Assess indication-specific symptom response, adherence, and adverse effects; screen bipolar history before starting.
Monitor worsening depression, suicidality, unusual behavior, and mania, especially during early treatment or dose changes.
Evaluate suspected serotonin syndrome, bleeding, or symptomatic hyponatremia promptly. Consider sodium assessment when risk or symptoms warrant it.
Monitor pediatric growth and weight; ask directly about sexual adverse effects.
Check INR with warfarin and phenytoin concentrations as indicated; review hepatic function and cardiac-risk context.
Take the prescribed once-daily dose. If a dose is missed, take it when remembered unless nearly time for the next; do not double.
Do not abruptly stop. Contact the prescriber for a taper or troublesome adverse effects.
Review all medicines and supplements, including pain relievers and St. John’s wort; avoid alcohol.
Do not drive or operate hazardous machinery until the effect on alertness is known.
Dilute the concentrate only with the specified liquids and take immediately. Review latex sensitivity and disulfiram use.
Report suicidal thoughts, marked mood changes, severe rash, eye pain or visual changes, or signs of serotonin syndrome urgently.
For overdose, contact U.S. Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 or seek emergency assessment.
Other manufacturers and formulations differ. Confirm the imprint and original packaging with a pharmacist.
Dosage form / strength: Film-coated scored tablet · 50 mg
Label distributor: Viatris Specialty LLC
Appearance: Light blue, capsular-shaped tablet
Imprint: ZOLOFT on one side · 50 mg on the scored side
Example package NDC: 58151-575-93 · 30 tablets
Zoloft tablets: 25, 50, 100 mg
Zoloft oral concentrate: 20 mg/mL; 60 mL bottle; 12% alcohol; dilute before use
Other products: Generic tablets, other liquids, and capsule products require their own labels and instructions.

Store Zoloft at 20–25°C (68–77°F); excursions 15–30°C (59–86°F) are permitted. Keep the bottle tightly closed and medicines out of children’s reach. Mix the oral concentrate only immediately before the dose.

assertions: Lexapro is indicated for MDD in adults and patients aged 12 years or older, and GAD in adults and patients aged 7 years or older. It is an oral prescription medicine; these age limits do not establish effectiveness below the respective thresholds.

This profile follows the branded Lexapro label. Some generic labels may retain different pediatric indication wording. Other psychiatric uses require an indication-specific assessment and are not represented here as FDA-approved uses.

All listed populations start at 10 mg once daily; 20 mg once daily is the labeled maximum. Increase only after assessing response and tolerability. The adult MDD fixed-dose trial did not establish extra benefit at 20 mg over 10 mg.

Take once daily, morning or evening, with or without food. Lexapro tablets contain 5, 10 or 20 mg; the 10 and 20 mg tablets are scored. The label describes a 1 mg/mL oral solution but explicitly states that this branded solution is not currently marketed.

sourceAudit.card: Older adults, liver and kidney function
assertions: The recommended dose for most older patients and patients with hepatic impairment is 10 mg daily. Mild or moderate renal impairment needs no dose adjustment; dosing is undetermined at creatinine clearance below 20 mL/min, requiring caution and individualized review.

Reduce gradually whenever possible and monitor withdrawal symptoms. Intolerable symptoms may require returning to the prior dose followed by a slower reduction. Keep at least 14 days between stopping a psychiatric MAOI and starting escitalopram, or stopping escitalopram and starting a psychiatric MAOI.

Screen for bipolar disorder before treatment; activation of mania or hypomania can occur. Use cautiously with a seizure history. Hyponatremia, often involving SIADH, is more likely with older age, diuretics or volume depletion; confusion, weakness or unsteadiness warrant assessment, and severe cases can cause seizures.

Serotonin syndrome can occur alone or with serotonergic combinations. Fever, agitation, tremor, hyperreflexia or diarrhea with clinical deterioration require urgent care; stop implicated drugs and provide supportive treatment when syndrome is diagnosed. Bleeding risk rises with drugs affecting hemostasis. Anatomically narrow untreated eye angles confer an angle-closure risk.

QT effects depend on dose. UK MHRA advice prohibits use with known or congenital QT prolongation or other QT-prolonging medicines; it recommends considering ECG review in cardiac disease, correcting potassium or magnesium deficits, and ECG assessment for palpitations or syncope. These are UK restrictions, distinct from the U.S. contraindication list.

Do not combine with psychiatric MAOIs or use within the 14-day washout in either direction. Do not initiate during linezolid or intravenous methylene blue treatment. Pimozide coadministration and hypersensitivity to escitalopram, citalopram or ingredients are contraindications.

sourceAudit.card: Boxed warning · Suicidal thoughts and behaviors
assertions: Antidepressant trials show increased suicidal thoughts and behaviors in pediatric and young adult patients. Monitor every treated patient for worsening mood or new suicidality, especially early in treatment and after dose changes; patients and caregivers should promptly report changes.

Common trial effects include nausea, insomnia, sweating, fatigue, somnolence and sexual dysfunction. Ask about baseline and emerging sexual concerns. Postmarketing reports include QT prolongation and torsades de pointes; spontaneous reports do not establish their frequency.

Overdose can produce delayed seizures, QRS/QT changes and arrhythmias. Urgent poison-center or emergency assessment is needed; cardiac monitoring may need to continue after an apparently mild early presentation.

Review other SSRIs/SNRIs, triptans, tramadol, fentanyl, lithium, buspirone, amphetamines, tryptophan and St. John’s wort for serotonin toxicity. MAOIs, linezolid/IV methylene blue and pimozide require the restrictions above. Do not duplicate escitalopram with citalopram.

NSAIDs, aspirin, antiplatelet drugs and anticoagulants increase bleeding risk; monitor INR carefully when warfarin is used. Escitalopram can increase exposure to CYP2D6 substrates, exemplified by desipramine. Review QT-prolonging medicines and electrolyte-depleting drugs using the applicable local cardiac guidance.

Available human data have not established an increased risk of major birth defects or miscarriage. Late exposure can involve neonatal poor adaptation or persistent pulmonary hypertension; use near delivery is associated with postpartum bleeding risk. Discuss untreated illness, relapse and neonatal planning; avoid unsupervised abrupt cessation.

Escitalopram and its metabolite enter milk. LactMed reports low exposure with maternal doses up to 20 mg/day and says a needed treatment is not itself a reason to stop breastfeeding. Monitor infant sedation, restlessness, feeding and weight gain, especially in young exclusively breastfed infants or with multiple psychotropics.

Follow the diagnosis-specific age approval. Monitor height and weight in pediatric patients because appetite and weight changes can occur. Older patients have higher exposure and a greater risk of clinically important hyponatremia; the usual recommended dose is 10 mg daily.

Use the hepatic and renal dosing distinctions above. Recently infarcted or unstable cardiac patients were not systematically evaluated in the clinical program; review cardiovascular status and interacting drugs rather than assuming trial safety generalizes to every cardiac condition.
Escitalopram is the S-enantiomer of citalopram. Its antidepressant activity is associated with potentiating central serotonergic signaling through inhibition of serotonin reuptake.

Peak concentrations follow an oral dose at about 5 hours; food does not materially alter absorption. Protein binding is about 56%. CYP2C19 and CYP3A4 contribute to hepatic metabolism. Terminal half-life is approximately 27–32 hours and steady state is reached in about a week.

Confirm diagnosis, bipolar/mania history, suicidality, interacting drugs and relevant cardiac or electrolyte risk. Follow mood, function, activation, adverse effects and sexual health. Check sodium when symptoms or risk factors warrant it; pediatric growth requires follow-up.

Take consistently and follow a clinician-directed taper. Avoid driving until the individual response is known; concomitant alcohol use is not advised. Report new suicidality, severe agitation with fever, abnormal bleeding, eye pain or new visual symptoms, fainting, confusion or seizures promptly.

Lexapro 10 mg tablets: white to off-white, round and scored, with F/L on the scored side and 10 on the other. Example bottle of 100: NDC 0456-2010-01. Generic appearance differs; verify the package and manufacturer.

assertions: Ozempic injection treats adult type 2 diabetes alongside diet and exercise; it also reduces major cardiovascular events in adults with type 2 diabetes and established cardiovascular disease, and specified kidney/CV outcomes in adults with type 2 diabetes and CKD. Rybelsus and Ozempic tablets treat adult type 2 diabetes and reduce major cardiovascular events in adults with type 2 diabetes at high cardiovascular risk. The oral diabetes label does not establish the injection’s kidney-outcome indication.

Wegovy injection and tablets are adjuncts to reduced-calorie nutrition and activity for adult weight reduction and long-term maintenance in obesity, or overweight with at least one weight-related condition. Both reduce major cardiovascular events in adults with established cardiovascular disease and obesity or overweight. Only Wegovy injection has the pediatric weight indication, for age 12 years or older with obesity.

Wegovy injection treats adults with noncirrhotic metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis and moderate-to-advanced fibrosis (F2–F3). This is accelerated approval based on histologic improvement; continued approval may depend on confirmation of clinical benefit. The MASH indication does not apply to oral Wegovy or the 7.2 mg weight-management regimen. Ozempic is not approved as a weight-management or MASH product.

Start 0.25 mg subcutaneously once weekly for 4 weeks, then 0.5 mg weekly. For additional glucose control, increase to 1 mg after at least 4 weeks at 0.5 mg, then to 2 mg after at least 4 weeks at 1 mg. The maximum is 2 mg weekly. For the type 2 diabetes/CKD outcome indication, use 1 mg weekly after at least 4 weeks at 0.5 mg.

Take only one prescribed tablet each day. The initial 30-day doses below are initiation doses and are not effective doses for glycemic control. These two formulations cannot be substituted milligram for milligram.

rows: 7 mg; increase to 14 mg if needed
4 mg; increase to 9 mg if needed

assertions: Weekly escalation is 0.25 mg for weeks 1–4, 0.5 mg for weeks 5–8, 1 mg for weeks 9–12 and 1.7 mg for weeks 13–16. If a dose is poorly tolerated, consider delaying the next step by 4 weeks. Choose the maintenance regimen by indication.

rows: 2.4 mg recommended or 1.7 mg weekly; if additional reduction needed and 2.4 mg tolerated ≥4 weeks, may increase to 7.2 mg
2.4 mg weekly; reduce to 1.7 mg if needed for tolerance and consider re-escalation

assertions: For adult weight management or cardiovascular risk reduction, take 1.5 mg daily for days 1–30, 4 mg for days 31–60, 9 mg for days 61–90, then 25 mg daily from day 91. Delay escalation if needed for GI tolerance. If 25 mg cannot be tolerated, consider the labeled switch to 1.7 mg weekly injection. Oral Wegovy is not a pediatric or MASH regimen.

Inject weekly into abdomen, thigh or upper arm, rotating sites; meals do not determine injection timing. Do not mix with insulin; use separate nonadjacent sites. Oral products require an empty stomach in the morning with plain water, no more than 4 ounces; swallow whole and wait at least 30 minutes before food, other drinks or oral medicines. Do not crush, split or dissolve tablets.

Ozempic injection: take within 5 days of the missed dose, otherwise skip; changing the weekly day requires more than 48 hours between injections. Wegovy injection: take a missed dose if the next is more than 2 days away, or skip if less than 2 days away; after two or more consecutive missed doses, reinitiate escalation at a lower dose. A missed oral dose is skipped; take the next tablet the following day.

Use only the label-supported transition. After the initiation phase, Rybelsus 7 mg corresponds to Ozempic tablets 4 mg, and Rybelsus 14 mg to Ozempic tablets 9 mg; start the new formulation the next day. The combined oral label provides transitions from Ozempic injection 0.5 mg one week later to Rybelsus 7 or 14 mg daily or Ozempic tablets 4 or 9 mg daily. For adult Wegovy weight/CV therapy, transition from 2.4 mg injection to 25 mg oral one week later, or from 25 mg oral to 2.4 mg weekly injection the next day (consider 1.7 mg if 25 mg is not tolerated). Do not invent equivalence for other doses or brands.

Stop and assess suspected pancreatitis. Persistent vomiting or diarrhea can cause volume depletion and acute kidney injury; monitor renal function when these occur, especially during escalation. Severe GI reactions occur; the reviewed products are not recommended in severe gastroparesis. Gallbladder symptoms warrant investigation.

Rapid glucose improvement may worsen existing diabetic retinopathy; monitor patients with a history. Insulin or sulfonylureas increase hypoglycemia risk. Hypersensitivity can be serious. Pulmonary aspiration has been reported during general anesthesia or deep sedation despite fasting; alert the procedural team. Labels do not establish a universally effective hold interval or fasting modification. Never share an injection pen.

Monitor heart rate during Wegovy treatment; sustained resting increases warrant discontinuation. The June 2026 label no longer includes the prior suicidality warning. FDA’s January 2026 review found no increased risk and requested removal; do not carry forward the superseded avoidance instruction.

EMA identifies non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy as a very rare semaglutide adverse effect. Sudden vision loss or rapidly worsening sight needs prompt assessment; EMA advises stopping semaglutide if NAION is confirmed. This is European regulatory guidance, distinct from the diabetic-retinopathy warning in the reviewed U.S. labels.

Personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma, MEN2, and a prior serious hypersensitivity reaction to semaglutide or the particular product’s ingredients are contraindications. Wegovy’s separate limitations-of-use statement says coadministration with other semaglutide products or another GLP-1 receptor agonist is not recommended.

Semaglutide causes thyroid C-cell tumors in rodents; relevance to humans is unknown. Counsel about a neck mass, persistent hoarseness or difficulty swallowing or breathing. Routine calcitonin testing or thyroid ultrasound has uncertain value for early detection; investigate concerning findings rather than treating screening as mandatory.

Nausea, vomiting and diarrhea are prominent; abdominal symptoms and constipation also occur. Frequency and severity vary by dose, route and study population. Ileus, intestinal obstruction and severe constipation have been reported after approval; spontaneous reports do not establish incidence.

Altered skin sensation (dysesthesia) was more frequent in Wegovy 7.2 mg trials. In those trials, dose reduction or interruption was often followed by recovery; persistent or intolerable symptoms need clinical review.

Hypoglycemia risk increases with insulin or sulfonylureas; reducing their dose may be necessary. Educate patients about recognition and management, and reassess glucose after starting or increasing semaglutide.

Delayed gastric emptying can affect oral drug absorption. Monitor medicines with narrow therapeutic ranges or those needing clinical or laboratory surveillance. Oral semaglutide must precede other oral medicines by at least 30 minutes; the oral labels report increased thyroxine exposure with levothyroxine and support thyroid-parameter monitoring. Avoid duplicate semaglutide prescriptions; Wegovy’s label recommends against concurrent semaglutide or other GLP-1 therapy.

Plan discontinuation at least 2 months before intended pregnancy because elimination is prolonged. For Wegovy weight/CV use, discontinue when pregnancy is recognized. Wegovy MASH and Ozempic/Rybelsus diabetes treatment require an individualized benefit–fetal-risk assessment; limited human data and adverse animal findings preclude assuming safety. Arrange alternative disease management.

Breastfeeding is not recommended with the reviewed oral products because their absorption enhancer, SNAC, enters milk and infant accumulation is a concern. Injection does not contain this enhancer; its labeling calls for weighing maternal treatment need, breastfeeding benefits and potential infant risk. Do not apply the oral restriction automatically to injectable therapy.

Only the lower-dose Wegovy injection weight regimen is approved from age 12 years for obesity. Pediatric use of oral Wegovy, Wegovy 7.2 mg, Ozempic and Rybelsus is not established. In the Wegovy cardiovascular trial, patients aged 75 or older had more hip/pelvic fractures and more serious adverse reactions; assess tolerance and individual risks.

sourceAudit.card: Renal, hepatic and oral Wegovy evidence limits
assertions: Ozempic injection and the oral diabetes label recommend no renal or hepatic dose adjustment, including renal failure in their reviewed pharmacokinetic data. Wegovy reports no clinically important exposure differences across the studied renal range (eGFR 30 to below 90) or hepatic impairment; this does not establish equivalent evidence in every advanced kidney population. Acute volume depletion still requires renal monitoring. Oral Wegovy was not studied for weight reduction in type 2 diabetes and has lower, more variable exposure in that population; consider alternative therapy or injection for inadequate response.

GLP-1 receptor activation increases glucose-dependent insulin secretion, suppresses inappropriate glucagon and delays gastric emptying. Reduced energy intake contributes to weight effects. Clinical outcome indications depend on the product’s trials and approval, rather than the shared mechanism alone.

Semaglutide is more than 99% protein bound and has an approximately 1-week half-life. It undergoes proteolytic cleavage and fatty-acid-chain metabolism, with metabolites eliminated in urine and feces. Subcutaneous bioavailability is about 89%; injection peak timing is about 1–3 days. Oral SNAC formulations enhance stomach absorption, with exposure dependent on administration conditions.

Track glycemic response in diabetes, weight response in weight management and the relevant disease outcomes for the approved indication. Assess GI tolerance, hydration, glucose-lowering co-therapy and retinopathy history; check renal function when volume depletion occurs. Monitor resting heart rate on Wegovy. MASH treatment requires specialist assessment of disease stage and ongoing benefit.

Confirm the prescribed brand, route, strength and escalation step at each refill. Demonstrate the exact device or oral fasting routine. Seek urgent assessment for severe persistent abdominal pain, inability to retain fluids, allergic symptoms or sudden visual loss. Tell anesthesia and sedation teams about semaglutide and follow their individualized instructions. Do not share pens or add another semaglutide product.

Suspected overdose requires poison-center or urgent medical assessment and supportive management. Severe nausea, vomiting or hypoglycemia may need prolonged observation because semaglutide’s half-life is about 1 week.

Example Wegovy 25 mg oral bottle: NDC 0169-4425-31. Its tablets bear strength and Novo markings. Some other semaglutide tablets have overlapping appearance; identify by the labeled brand, strength and NDC.

assertions: Ozempic multidose pens deliver 0.25/0.5, 1 or 2 mg; current single-dose syringes contain 0.25, 0.5 or 1 mg. Wegovy single-dose pens include 0.25, 0.5, 1, 1.7, 2.4 and 7.2 mg; single-dose syringes do not include 7.2 mg. Wegovy FlexTouch contains four 2.4 mg doses (9.6 mg/3 mL). Follow device-specific training; visually impaired patients should not self-administer FlexTouch without appropriate assistance.
Rybelsus tablets contain 3, 7 or 14 mg; Ozempic tablets contain 1.5, 4 or 9 mg; Wegovy tablets contain 1.5, 4, 9 or 25 mg. These products are not milligram-for-milligram substitutes.

assertions: Before use, refrigerate at 2–8°C and never freeze. Ozempic multidose pens can remain in use for 56 days at 15–30°C or refrigerated; remove the needle between uses. Ozempic single-dose syringes and Wegovy single-dose devices permit up to 28 days at 8–30°C under the labeled conditions; protect from light in the carton. Wegovy FlexTouch permits 56 days after first use at 15–30°C or refrigerated, with needle removed. Distinguish devices rather than applying one storage interval to every injection.

Store tablets at 20–25°C, allowing excursions to 15–30°C, in the original bottle to protect from moisture. This reference covers the cited U.S. branded products and current labeling; it does not provide compounded-product dosing or establish availability in every jurisdiction.

assertions: Immediate-release Adderall is labeled for ADHD and narcolepsy. Its ADHD dosing begins at age 3; use below age 3 is not recommended. Adderall XR is labeled for ADHD in adults and children age 6 years and older; use below age 6 is not recommended because of higher exposure and adverse reactions.

Narcolepsy is not an Adderall XR-labeled indication. These profiles concern the named mixed-salt products, not every amphetamine preparation. Treatment requires a confirmed diagnosis and an individualized care plan.

Both reviewed U.S. products are prescription-only Schedule II medicines. The representative Teva IR label carries marketing application ANDA040422; the Takeda XR label carries NDA021303. Approval does not remove the risks of misuse, addiction, or serious adverse reactions.

The IR label does not provide a separate adult ADHD starting-dose schedule. Individualize adult dosing with the prescriber; do not import XR directions or treat the narcolepsy range as an ADHD allowance. Avoid late-evening IR doses.
Children age 3–5 | Start 2.5 mg daily; increase by 2.5 mg/day at weekly intervals if needed.
Children age 6 and older | Start 5 mg once or twice daily; increase by 5 mg/day at weekly intervals if needed.
Daily dose / timing | The label says exceeding 40 mg/day is rarely necessary for ADHD. First dose on awakening; additional doses, if prescribed, 4–6 hours apart.

The usual labeled range is 5–60 mg/day in divided doses. For age 12 years and older, the label specifies a 10 mg daily start with 10 mg/day weekly increases as needed. Its pediatric wording also suggests 5 mg daily for ages 6–12 with 5 mg/day weekly increments; the age-12 overlap should be resolved with the treating specialist rather than selecting a dose from this summary. Subsequent doses, if prescribed, are 4–6 hours apart; reduce for troublesome insomnia or anorexia.

Use the lowest effective dose and titrate weekly. When switching from divided-dose Adderall IR, the XR label permits the same total daily dose once each morning; conversion requires prescriber review of renal function and the age-specific limits.
Age 6–12 | Start 10 mg each morning; 5 mg may be appropriate. Increase by 5 or 10 mg/day weekly. Maximum recommended 30 mg/day.
Age 13–17 | Start 10 mg each morning; may increase to 20 mg/day after 1 week if needed.
Adults | Recommended dose 20 mg each morning. This is a recommended dose, not a universal maximum derived from a trial.

Swallow the capsule whole, or open it and sprinkle all beads on applesauce. Consume immediately without chewing and do not store the mixture. Do not divide a capsule’s contents. Take on awakening, with or without food; avoid afternoon doses.

For XR with severe renal impairment (GFR 15 to <30 mL/min/1.73 m²): adults 15 mg each morning; ages 6–17 start at 5 mg each morning, with a maximum of 20 mg/day for ages 6–12. XR is not recommended with GFR <15.

These XR instructions are not an IR renal schedule. The IR label supplies no defined renal or hepatic reduction regimen. Either impairment may prolong amphetamine exposure; hepatic dosing is not quantified in the reviewed labels. Individualize therapy with the prescriber.

Avoid use with serious cardiac disease, including structural abnormalities, cardiomyopathy, serious arrhythmias, or coronary artery disease. Check cardiac history, family history, and examination before treatment; monitor blood pressure and pulse throughout.

Stimulants may worsen psychosis or induce mania; screen for bipolar risk. New hallucinations or manic symptoms warrant reassessment and possible discontinuation. Monitor height, weight, appetite, tics, and Tourette symptoms. Seizures warrant discontinuation. Check fingers and toes for Raynaud symptoms, ulcers, or other vascular changes.
Serotonin syndrome can include agitation, fever, sweating, unstable blood pressure, rigidity, twitching, and diarrhea. Stop implicated therapy and obtain urgent care if suspected.
Hypersensitivity to amphetamine or formulation components.
Concurrent MAOI use, or use within 14 days after stopping an MAOI, including linezolid or IV methylene blue; risk of hypertensive crisis.

sourceAudit.card_title: Boxed warning · Abuse, misuse, and addiction
assertions: Both products have high potential for abuse and misuse, which can cause a substance use disorder, including addiction. Misuse can cause overdose and death, especially with higher doses or unapproved administration. Assess risk before treatment; counsel about locked storage and disposal; reassess risk and monitor for misuse throughout treatment. Physical dependence and withdrawal can also occur; plan changes with the prescriber.

Common reactions vary by age and include reduced appetite, insomnia, abdominal discomfort, weight loss, dry mouth, headache, anxiety, and tachycardia. Serious hypersensitivity, severe psychiatric symptoms, and cardiovascular or neurologic emergencies require assessment.
Suspected overdose needs immediate medical help; XR effects may be prolonged. Contact U.S. Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222. Call 911 for collapse, seizure, trouble breathing, or inability to awaken.
MAOIs: contraindicated concurrently and for 14 days after discontinuation.

Serotonergic drugs or CYP2D6 inhibitors: increased serotonin-syndrome risk and possible higher exposure. Consider alternatives; if necessary, initiate at a lower dose and monitor closely during initiation and titration.
Gastrointestinal or urinary alkalinizing agents: increase exposure. XR labeling advises avoiding both; IR labeling explicitly advises avoiding gastrointestinal alkalinizing agents.
Acidifying agents, including those used with methenamine: may reduce exposure and efficacy. Adjust only under prescriber supervision based on response.
Tricyclic antidepressants can potentiate cardiovascular effects; monitor frequently and adjust or use an alternative.
PPIs may shorten time to peak effect; monitor for a change in clinical response.
IR label also describes reduced antihypertensive effects and interactions with antihistamines, antipsychotics, anticonvulsants, lithium, and adrenergic medicines; review the full medication list.

Amphetamines can affect corticosteroid and urinary steroid tests. The current XR label also describes interference with ioflupane I-123 dopamine-transporter imaging; coordinate an adequate washout with the imaging and prescribing teams rather than stopping independently.

Review maternal benefit and fetal risk with the obstetric and prescribing clinicians. XR labeling states that available epidemiologic data have not identified a major birth-defect or miscarriage risk, while premature delivery and low birth weight have been reported. This does not establish absence of risk. Monitor exposed newborns for withdrawal or feeding difficulties. The IR label uses older pregnancy wording and advises use only when benefit justifies risk.

Both product labels advise against breastfeeding during treatment. Amphetamine reaches milk; long-term infant neurodevelopmental effects remain uncertain and high doses may reduce milk supply. LactMed reports that some experts allow prescribed therapeutic doses with infant monitoring for irritability, insomnia, and feeding difficulty. This requires an individualized clinical decision; breastfeeding is discouraged with active amphetamine misuse.

Do not substitute IR’s age-3 ADHD directions for XR’s age-6 indication. Monitor pediatric height and weight and consider interruption when growth is inadequate. The reviewed labels state that geriatric use has not been studied; reassess cardiovascular risks and suitability rather than extrapolating pediatric regimens.

Reduced elimination may increase exposure. Follow the explicit XR severe-renal and ESRD instructions; no fixed IR renal or hepatic regimen is supplied. Dialysis does not reliably remove d-amphetamine.

Amphetamines are sympathomimetic CNS stimulants. They increase extracellular norepinephrine and dopamine through effects on release and reuptake; the precise therapeutic mechanism in ADHD is not established.
Peak concentration: About 3 hours for IR; about 7 hours for XR. Food can delay XR peak timing.
Adult half-life: XR data: approximately 10 hours for d-amphetamine and 13 hours for l-amphetamine.
Metabolism / elimination: Hepatic metabolism includes CYP2D6; renal excretion depends strongly on urine pH. Alkaline urine reduces elimination; acidic urine increases it.
Before treatment: confirm the indication; assess cardiac and family history, examination, bipolar or psychosis risk, tics, and misuse risk.
During treatment and dose changes: assess function and symptom benefit, blood pressure, pulse, appetite, sleep, mood, tics, growth, and digital circulation.
Reassess misuse, diversion, and addiction risk frequently; review refill patterns, storage, and all interacting medicines.

sections: Assessment and monitoring of misuse risk

assertions: Use exactly as prescribed. Never share; keep in a secure, preferably locked location and follow safe disposal instructions.
Check the bottle for IR versus XR. Do not crush or chew XR beads or divide a capsule.
If an XR morning dose is missed, skip it and take the next morning’s scheduled dose; do not take it later or double it. For IR missed doses, follow the prescriber’s timing plan.
Seek urgent care for chest pain, shortness of breath, unexplained fainting, serotonin-syndrome symptoms, or serious allergy; promptly report hallucinations, mania, or finger/toe wounds.
Discuss pregnancy, breastfeeding, and stopping or reducing prolonged treatment with the prescriber.

assertions: Protonix oral products are labeled for short-term healing and symptom relief of GERD-associated erosive esophagitis in adults and children age 5 and older; maintenance of healed erosive esophagitis and reduced heartburn relapse in adults; and long-term treatment of pathological hypersecretory conditions, including Zollinger–Ellison syndrome, in adults.
Maintenance trials did not extend beyond 12 months. The pediatric indication is erosive esophagitis, not every reflux symptom; other pediatric uses are not established by this label.

Protonix IV is labeled for GERD with a history of erosive esophagitis for up to 10 days in adults and up to 7 days in children age 3 months and older, and for pathological hypersecretory conditions in adults. Switch to an appropriate oral medicine as soon as tolerated. The IV label states that efficacy and safety for upper GI bleeding have not been established; that is distinct from clinician-directed off-label protocols.
Erosive esophagitis | 40 mg once daily for up to 8 weeks; an additional 8 weeks may be considered in adults not healed.
Maintenance of healing | 40 mg once daily; controlled trials did not exceed 12 months.
Pathological hypersecretion | 40 mg twice daily initially; individualize to response for as long as indicated. Doses up to 240 mg/day have been administered.

Safety beyond 8 weeks is not established in children. The 40 mg packet is a fixed dose and must not be divided to make 20 mg; use an appropriate tablet or obtain a different clinician-directed plan. The table supplies no regimen for a child below 15 kg.
15 to <40 kg | 20 mg
≥40 kg | 40 mg

Swallow whole with or without food; do not split, crush, or chew. Two 20 mg tablets may replace one 40 mg tablet if swallowing the larger tablet is difficult. Antacids do not affect tablet absorption.

Take approximately 30 minutes before a meal. Sprinkle the whole packet on 1 teaspoon of applesauce and swallow within 10 minutes without chewing; follow with sips of water. Alternatively, mix the whole packet with 1 teaspoon of apple juice, stir for 5 seconds, swallow immediately, and rinse the container once or twice with apple juice to take all granules.

Do not use other foods or liquids, and do not crush or chew the granules. NG or gastrostomy administration requires apple juice and a tube of at least 16 French; follow the full label’s syringe and repeated-rinse instructions with professional guidance.

Hepatic impairment substantially increases exposure, although accumulation with once-daily dosing is limited. Symptom improvement does not exclude gastric malignancy. A poor response or early relapse after treatment requires further evaluation. Acute tubulointerstitial nephritis can occur at any time, even without rash or fever; stop and evaluate if suspected.

Persistent diarrhea may indicate C. difficile infection. Stop and assess severe skin or hypersensitivity reactions; PPIs have been associated with lupus. Prolonged or multiple-daily-dose use is associated with fracture risk in observational studies. Long-term therapy can cause vitamin B12 deficiency, hypomagnesemia with other mineral disturbances, and fundic gland polyps. Individualize duration rather than continuing without an indication.
Hypersensitivity to pantoprazole, any formulation component, or substituted benzimidazoles is a contraindication. Do not combine with rilpivirine-containing medicines.

assertions: Common adult reactions include headache, diarrhea, nausea, abdominal pain, vomiting, flatulence, dizziness, and joint pain. Pediatric oral trial reactions also included upper respiratory infection, fever, and rash. These trial observations do not establish an individual’s risk.

IV treatment can cause injection-site reactions. Its EDTA ingredient can worsen zinc deficiency in susceptible patients; consider supplementation when appropriate. Follow IV compatibility instructions, including incompatibility with Y-site midazolam and potential incompatibility with zinc-containing products. Rodent tumor findings in the oral label have uncertain relevance to human cancer.
Rilpivirine-containing products: contraindicated. Avoid nelfinavir; consult atazanavir dosing instructions. Monitor saquinavir toxicity when relevant.
Warfarin: possible INR or prothrombin-time elevation; monitor and adjust warfarin as needed.
High-dose methotrexate: possible prolonged exposure and toxicity; consider a temporary PPI hold with the treating team.
Acid-dependent absorption: review iron, azole antifungals, selected kinase inhibitors, and other affected medicines using their exact labels.
Mycophenolate mofetil: exposure to active mycophenolic acid may decrease; use caution in transplant patients. A rejection effect is not established by the Protonix label.
Clopidogrel: the label reports no clinically important interaction at approved pantoprazole doses; no clopidogrel dose adjustment is required on that basis.

Pantoprazole can raise chromogranin A and confound neuroendocrine-tumor testing. The label advises a clinician-directed hold of at least 14 days before testing, with repeat testing if still high and the same laboratory for serial measurements. False-positive urine THC screening has been reported; confirm positive screens using an alternative method.

Available observational human data have not shown an association with major malformations or other adverse pregnancy outcomes. Animal developmental findings include bone changes in offspring; the labels advise counseling about potential fetal harm. Review the indication and alternatives with the obstetric clinician rather than asserting proven safety.

Pantoprazole reaches milk in low amounts. The label recommends balancing maternal clinical need, breastfeeding benefits, and possible infant effects. Current LactMed expects no adverse effects from maternal 40 mg daily based on low milk exposure, while infant blood-level and outcome evidence remains limited.

Oral products are indicated from age 5 for short-term erosive esophagitis; the marketed strengths do not provide an appropriate formulation below age 5. Pediatric oral maintenance or hypersecretory indications are not established. IV has a separate GERD/history-of-EE indication from age 3 months. Follow its distinct weight boundaries and 7-day limit.
Older adults had generally comparable short-term efficacy and safety in the oral trials; assess comorbidity, fracture risk, and persistent symptoms rather than making an age-only dosing change.

Renal impairment does not eliminate the possibility of PPI-associated acute nephritis. Hepatic impairment increases exposure; high oral doses above 40 mg/day are not studied in that group. Review prolonged or intensive dosing with the treating clinician.

Pantoprazole covalently binds gastric parietal-cell H+/K+-ATPase, inhibiting the final step in basal and stimulated acid secretion. The effect persists beyond 24 hours at studied doses despite a short circulating half-life.
Absorption: Enteric coating delays tablet absorption until after gastric transit. Tablet peak concentration is about 2.5 hours; bioavailability about 77%.
Metabolism: Extensive hepatic metabolism, principally CYP2C19 with additional CYP3A4 pathways.
Elimination: Terminal plasma half-life about 1 hour in normal metabolizers; metabolites are eliminated mainly in urine. Hepatic impairment and poor CYP2C19 metabolism prolong exposure.
Confirm the indication and planned review date; assess symptom response and relapse, with diagnostic follow-up for persistent or recurrent symptoms.
Assess magnesium before and periodically during prolonged therapy or with digoxin/diuretics when appropriate; assess magnesium and calcium with preexisting hypocalcemia risk.
Evaluate B12 deficiency when suggestive symptoms occur during long-term therapy; assess fracture risk and possible nephritis or persistent diarrhea.
Monitor INR with warfarin; coordinate methotrexate, transplant-drug, and diagnostic-testing plans. Follow IV site reactions and zinc risk during IV treatment.
Keep tablets and granules intact; use the formulation-specific meal and mixing instructions. Do not split a granule packet for a smaller dose.
Take the missed oral dose when remembered unless nearly time for the next; skip then, and do not take two doses together.
Report persistent watery diarrhea, reduced urine, severe or blistering rash, sun-sensitive rash or joint pain, or symptoms suggesting low magnesium such as palpitations or muscle spasms.
Seek emergency care for serious allergy or severe acute symptoms. Discuss the need for continued treatment and all prescription/OTC medicines at follow-up.

IR
Start 100 mg twice daily; after 3 days may use 100 mg three times daily. Separate doses by ≥6 hours. Maximum 450 mg/day in divided doses, ≤150 mg each; increases ≤100 mg/day within 3 days.
Wellbutrin SR
Start 150 mg each morning; after 3 days may increase to 150 mg twice daily, ≥8 hours apart. After several weeks without response, up to 200 mg twice daily; maximum 400 mg/day and 200 mg/dose.

Start 150 mg each morning; after 4 days may increase to 300 mg each morning. This reference supplies no escalation above 300 mg because the selected source has conflicting dose-limit statements.

Start 150 mg each morning in autumn before symptoms; after 7 days may increase to 300 mg. Continue through winter and individualize spring taper; reduce 300 mg to 150 mg before stopping. Above 300 mg was not assessed in SAD trials.

Start 150 mg daily for 3 days, then 150 mg twice daily ≥8 hours apart; maximum 300 mg/day. Start before the quit day, setting it within the first 2 weeks. Usually treat 7–12 weeks with support; if not abstinent by then, reassess and usually discontinue. Longer treatment is individualized.

Child-Pugh 7–15: IR maximum 75 mg/day; depression SR 100 mg/day or 150 mg every other day; XL and smoking-cessation SR 150 mg every other day. With mild hepatic impairment consider lower dose/frequency. The selected IR, depression SR, Wellbutrin XL and cessation SR labels advise considering reduced dose/frequency when GFR <90 mL/min and monitoring for accumulation.

Swallow tablets whole; do not crush, split or chew. Take XL in the morning; food is optional. Clinician-directed switching to XL uses the same total daily dose when possible within product limits. Allow ≥14 days between bupropion and a psychiatric MAOI in either direction; urgent linezolid/IV methylene blue needs a specialist interruption and monitoring plan.

Seizure risk rises with dose and with head injury, CNS lesions, stroke, hypoxia, metabolic disturbance, alcohol/sedative misuse or other seizure-threshold-lowering medicines. Stop and do not restart after seizure. Monitor BP; screen for bipolar disorder. Mania, psychosis and serious behavioral changes may occur; stop and contact the clinician for concerning symptoms during a quit attempt. Narrow-angle glaucoma and severe allergic/skin reactions require urgent assessment.

Seizure disorder; current/prior anorexia nervosa or bulimia; abrupt withdrawal from alcohol, benzodiazepines, barbiturates or antiepileptics; hypersensitivity; psychiatric MAOIs concurrently or within 14 days in either direction. Do not start while receiving linezolid or IV methylene blue. Do not combine bupropion-containing products.

claims: The tablet label covers hypertension alone or with other antihypertensives, and adjunctive edema treatment associated with heart failure, cirrhosis, corticosteroid/estrogen therapy or renal disorders. The selected 12.5 mg capsule label is for hypertension.

Tablet pediatric directions are based on experience rather than controlled trials; the capsule label states pediatric safety/effectiveness are unestablished. Hydrochlorothiazide reduces renal sodium/chloride reabsorption, increasing water excretion with possible potassium and magnesium loss. Diuresis starts around 2 hours, peaks around 4 hours and lasts 6–12 hours. Its precise antihypertensive mechanism is not established.

Not metabolized.

OCD ages 7–17: start 10 mg/day. Higher-weight children/adolescents may increase to 20 mg after 2 weeks; usual range 20–60 mg/day with later increases after several weeks. For adult MDD continuation after satisfactory daily treatment response, start the once-weekly capsule 7 days after the last daily 20 mg dose. Weekly and daily regimens are not interchangeable pill-for-pill; equivalence in maintaining response has not been established. If response is not maintained, the clinician may return to daily therapy. This is not a 90 mg daily regimen.

Bipolar I depression: adult initial oral combination generally 5 mg olanzapine plus 20 mg fluoxetine each evening; ages 10–17 generally 2.5 mg plus 20 mg. Adult treatment-resistant depression generally starts 5 mg plus 20 mg each evening. These are component regimens; fixed-dose Symbyax correspondence and titration require its separate label.

Use a lower or less frequent dose with hepatic impairment; consider the same in older adults or medically complex patients. A renal reduction is not routinely necessary in the cited label, including its small dialysis study. Individualize rather than assuming identical exposure in every patient.

Wait at least 14 days after stopping a psychiatric MAOI before starting fluoxetine, and at least 5 weeks after stopping fluoxetine before starting a psychiatric MAOI. Do not start fluoxetine during linezolid or IV methylene blue treatment. Urgent use of these drugs requires a prescriber-managed interruption and monitoring protocol from section 2.10.

QT prolongation and torsades have been reported. Review cardiac disease, electrolyte depletion, interacting drugs, and increased-exposure conditions; consider ECG monitoring in at-risk patients.
Use caution with seizures. Rash or unexplained allergic symptoms may require stopping therapy; severe swelling or breathing difficulty is urgent.
Hyponatremia can cause confusion, weakness, unsteadiness or seizures, particularly with older age, diuretics or volume depletion. Bleeding risk rises with anticoagulants/antiplatelets/NSAIDs.

sources.version: 2026 edition; asthma treatment tracks, technique, adherence, and reassessment.

assertions: The selected OTC nasal products relieve nasal allergy symptoms. Propionate Flonase Allergy Relief is for age 4 and older; furoate Flonase Sensimist is for age 2 and older. Both include itchy, watery eye relief in their age 12-and-older directions. Nasal products are not asthma treatment.

The selected propionate HFA inhaler is labeled for asthma maintenance from age 4; furoate Arnuity Ellipta from age 5. Neither treats an acute attack. This reference covers these four single-ingredient products; other devices, prescription nasal indications, and combination inhalers need their own labels.

Doses below are sprays into EACH nostril once daily. Shake propionate gently and Sensimist vigorously before use; prime and clean according to the specific package instructions. Adults should supervise children. Use the least dose that controls symptoms.
Propionate 50 mcg/spray, age ≥12 | Week 1: 2 sprays; weeks 2–6 months: 1 or 2. Consult a clinician after 6 months of daily use.
Propionate, age 4–11 | 1 spray; shortest needed duration. Ask the child’s clinician if use exceeds 2 months/year. Do not use under age 4.
Furoate 27.5 mcg/spray, age ≥12 | Week 1: 2 sprays; weeks 2–6 months: 1 or 2. Consult a clinician after 6 months of daily use.
Furoate, age 2–11 | 1 spray; shortest needed duration. Ask the child’s clinician if use exceeds 2 months/year. Do not use under age 2.

For age ≥12 not previously using an inhaled corticosteroid, the starting dose is 88 mcg twice daily, approximately 12 hours apart; prior therapy and severity determine other starting regimens. The maximum labeled dose is 880 mcg twice daily. Age 4–11: 88 mcg twice daily (two 44-mcg actuations each time). Titrate to the lowest effective dose after stability; full benefit may take 2 weeks or longer.

Arnuity: age ≥12 not using an inhaled corticosteroid starts 100 mcg once daily; prior therapy/severity affect other starts. If response is inadequate after 2 weeks, consider 200 mcg once daily, the maximum for this age group. Age 5–11: 50 mcg once daily. Take one actuation at the same time each day, no more than once every 24 hours.

HFA: shake for 5 seconds before each spray. Prime with four sprays before first use; prime with one spray if unused for more than 7 days or dropped. A valved holding chamber, with a mask when appropriate, can help young children. Ellipta: opening the cover prepares one dose; exhale away from the device, inhale steadily and deeply through the mouthpiece, and do not block its air vent. After either asthma inhaler, rinse the mouth and spit out the water.

Asthma inhalers can cause thrush, infection susceptibility, adrenal suppression, reduced bone density, impaired growth, glaucoma/cataracts, and paradoxical bronchospasm. Worsening breathing immediately after a dose requires stopping that inhaler and urgent assessment with appropriate rescue treatment. Exposure to chickenpox or measles and existing infections need clinician review. During systemic-steroid reduction, the propionate HFA label also calls for assessment of eosinophilia, vasculitic rash, worsening lung symptoms, cardiac complications, or neuropathy; causality is unestablished. Transfer from systemic steroids requires supervised tapering; adrenal insufficiency may emerge during illness or surgery.

Nasal labels caution against use before nasal injury/surgery heals. Review recurrent severe nosebleeds, a whistling nasal sound, vision changes, or symptoms unimproved after 7 days. Children may grow more slowly. Seek assessment after exposure to chickenpox, measles, or tuberculosis. Use all corticosteroids together only after medication review.

Do not use a product after hypersensitivity to its ingredients. Both asthma inhalers are contraindicated as primary treatment of status asthmaticus or acute episodes needing intensive care. Arnuity contains lactose with milk proteins and is contraindicated in severe milk-protein allergy. Nasal OTC labels additionally say not to use below their respective age limits, for asthma, or with unhealed nasal injury/surgery.
These selected labels do not contain a boxed warning. Their adrenal, infection, growth, eye, and hypersensitivity warnings remain clinically important.

Nasal irritation, stinging, and bleeding can occur. Inhaled products commonly report upper respiratory symptoms, throat irritation, headache, or oral candidiasis; serious hypersensitivity is possible. Chronic excessive dosing or inhibited metabolism can cause systemic steroid effects and adrenal suppression. Do not add extra maintenance doses for an attack; suspected overdose or systemic steroid toxicity requires assessment.

sections: Drug Facts / When using, Stop use
Drug Facts / When using, Stop use

assertions: Propionate HFA labeling advises against strong CYP3A4 inhibitors, including ritonavir and strong azole inhibitors, because systemic exposure and adrenal toxicity may increase. Arnuity advises caution with strong inhibitors, including ritonavir and ketoconazole. Nasal OTC labels require clinician/pharmacist review with HIV medicines such as ritonavir or oral ketoconazole. This is not an identical prohibition for every formulation.

Reconcile oral, injected, nasal, inhaled, and topical steroids. Nasal labels specifically direct review of other steroid medicines. Inhaler labels caution that systemic-steroid withdrawal and total corticosteroid exposure require individualized management.

Nasal labels advise consultation during pregnancy or breastfeeding. Both asthma labels have insufficient human pregnancy data and emphasize the risks of poorly controlled asthma. Human milk data are unavailable for these inhaled ingredients; HFA labeling notes that low plasma concentrations suggest low milk levels. Balance breastfeeding benefits, maternal treatment needs, and potential infant effects rather than declaring proven safety.

Respect the separate nasal and inhaler ages and doses above; monitor pediatric growth and use the lowest effective dose. Older adults need attention to bone and eye risks. Arnuity requires no age-based geriatric dose adjustment; individual inhaler selection also depends on the ability to use the device.

Arnuity requires no renal or mild hepatic dose adjustment; moderate/severe hepatic impairment increases systemic exposure, warranting caution and monitoring for steroid effects. Pediatric hepatic effects were not evaluated. Formal renal/hepatic PK studies were not performed for propionate HFA; its hepatic clearance supports closer monitoring with liver disease. The selected OTC nasal labels provide no organ-specific numeric regimen.

Both esters activate glucocorticoid pathways and reduce inflammatory activity. Their asthma benefit develops with regular use and may take 1–2 weeks or longer to maximize. Receptor-binding comparisons do not establish a clinical dose equivalence.

Swallowed propionate has very low oral bioavailability, but drug delivered to the lung can enter systemic circulation. Propionate and furoate undergo hepatic CYP3A4 metabolism. Furoate inhalation has an approximately 24-hour elimination phase half-life after repeated dosing; these kinetics do not justify swapping the nasal and pulmonary regimens.

Check control, reliever use, exacerbations, adherence, and device technique before stepping up treatment. GINA 2026 prefers an ICS–formoterol reliever strategy for many adults/adolescents; alternatives use a maintenance controller with a separate reliever. Fluticasone alone is not an ICS–formoterol rescue or maintenance-and-reliever inhaler. Coordinate the prescribed reliever and action plan with the clinician.

sections: Summary guide pp. 14, 21–25 / treatment tracks and reassessment

assertions: Demonstrate the exact nasal or inhaler technique; inspect dose counters and do not exceed labeled use. Check thrush, eye symptoms, growth, and systemic steroid effects as appropriate. Seek urgent care for severe breathing difficulty or allergy. A nasal spray that fails after a week or requires prolonged pediatric use needs review; persistent asthma symptoms need controller reassessment.

Examples are Flonase Allergy Relief propionate nasal spray, Flonase Sensimist furoate nasal spray, Prasco propionate HFA authorized generic, and Arnuity Ellipta furoate powder. The HFA product uses an orange actuator and peach cap (44-mcg, 120-actuation package NDC 66993-078-96); Arnuity uses a light-gray/orange inhaler (50-mcg, 30-blister package NDC 0173-0888-10). Appearance can vary across manufacturers; verify the package and dose counter.

Selected strengths: propionate nasal 50 mcg/spray; furoate nasal 27.5 mcg/spray; propionate HFA 44, 110, or 220 mcg per actuation (120 metered actuations); Arnuity 50, 100, or 200 mcg per blister. The 50-mcg Arnuity pack has 30 blisters; 100/200 also have 14-dose institutional packs. These are different formulations, not a substitution table.

Propionate nasal: 4–30°C. Sensimist: 15–30°C; do not refrigerate or freeze. HFA: 20–25°C, excursions 15–30°C, mouthpiece down; protect from excessive heat, do not puncture/incinerate, and discard at counter 000. Arnuity: 20–25°C, excursions 15–30°C, dry and protected from heat/sunlight; keep sealed in its tray until use and discard 6 weeks after opening or at counter 0, whichever comes first. Use each inhaler with its own supplied device components.

sources.title: EAU Guidelines on Urolithiasis · 2026
sources.note: Current 2026 guideline; sections 3.4.3 and 3.4.9.b, medical expulsive therapy.
sources.version: Current 2026 guideline; sections 3.4.3 and 3.4.9.b, medical expulsive therapy.

assertions: Flomax treats signs and symptoms of benign prostatic hyperplasia. It is not labeled to treat hypertension. Evaluate the cause of urinary symptoms because BPH and prostate cancer can coexist.

EAU 2026 offers alpha blockers as an off-label option for selected patients with distal ureteral stones 5–10 mm. Use only when active removal is not indicated and the patient understands the tradeoffs. Stop conservative treatment if infection, refractory pain, or worsening renal function develops. This guideline does not establish a U.S. tamsulosin approval or a universal stone-treatment dose.

Take 0.4 mg once daily about 30 minutes after the same meal each day. If response is insufficient after 2–4 weeks, the prescriber may increase to 0.8 mg once daily. If either regimen is interrupted for several days, restart with 0.4 mg once daily. Swallow capsules whole; do not open, crush, or chew.

No renal dose adjustment is specified, but CrCl below 10 mL/min/1.73 m² was not studied. Moderate hepatic impairment requires no adjustment; severe impairment was not studied. Review hypotension risk and interacting medicines before increasing to 0.8 mg.

Postural dizziness, hypotension, and syncope can occur; protect against falls especially when starting or restarting. Current or previous exposure can cause intraoperative floppy iris syndrome during cataract/glaucoma surgery. Do not start when such surgery is scheduled; the benefit of stopping beforehand is unproven, so coordinate rather than choosing a washout. A painful persistent erection needs immediate treatment. Screen for prostate cancer before therapy and periodically. Use caution after serious or life-threatening sulfonamide allergy.

Known hypersensitivity to tamsulosin or any capsule component is a contraindication. Strong CYP3A4 inhibitor combinations are directed against under dosage/warnings rather than listed in the formal contraindications section.
The selected U.S. label contains no boxed warning. Its syncope, interaction, priapism, and surgical warnings still require action.

Dizziness, abnormal ejaculation, rhinitis, and fatigue are reported in trials. Postmarketing reports include hypersensitivity, severe skin reactions, hypotension, arrhythmias, and IFIS; spontaneous reports cannot establish frequency. Excess dosing can cause marked hypotension requiring cardiovascular support, fluids or vasopressors as appropriate, and renal monitoring. Dialysis is unlikely to help because protein binding is high.

Do not combine with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors such as ketoconazole. Use caution with moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors (erythromycin), strong/moderate CYP2D6 inhibitors (paroxetine/terbinafine), known CYP2D6 poor metabolism, and cimetidine—especially above 0.4 mg. Simultaneous inhibition of both pathways may substantially increase exposure.

Do not combine with another alpha blocker. PDE5 inhibitors can produce symptomatic hypotension; review the combination and monitor. Warfarin interaction studies are inconclusive, and the label recommends caution rather than a predictable dose change.

Flomax is not indicated for women. Human pregnancy-risk and milk/infant-effect data are inadequate or absent; animal findings do not establish human safety. Ejaculatory changes can affect sexual function, and label fertility effects are based on animal studies, not a quantified human infertility risk. Off-label treatment during pregnancy or lactation requires a separate assessment.

There is no pediatric indication; trials in children with neurologic bladder dysfunction did not demonstrate efficacy. Older adults showed no overall trial difference, but greater sensitivity remains possible, warranting attention to dizziness and falls.

Renal impairment generally needs no dose adjustment; end-stage renal disease below CrCl 10 mL/min/1.73 m² remains unstudied. Moderate hepatic impairment needs no adjustment; no severe-hepatic regimen is established by the label.

Tamsulosin preferentially blocks alpha-1 receptors in the prostate, reducing the dynamic smooth-muscle component of bladder outlet obstruction and improving urine flow and BPH symptoms. This mechanism does not make it an approved antihypertensive.

Food changes absorption, supporting consistent meal timing. The drug is highly protein bound and metabolized mainly through CYP3A4 and CYP2D6. Less than 10% is excreted unchanged in urine. The apparent half-life with Flomax capsules is about 9–13 hours in healthy volunteers and 14–15 hours in the target population.

Assess urinary symptoms, response after the initial 2–4 weeks, blood-pressure symptoms, and medication interactions. Perform prostate-cancer assessment before treatment and periodically. Ask about cataract/glaucoma surgery, falls, severe sulfa allergy, and prior alpha-blocker exposure.

Rise carefully and avoid hazardous activities until the effect is known. Report fainting, troublesome ejaculation changes, or worsening urinary symptoms. Seek immediate help for a persistent painful erection, severe allergy, or severe skin reaction. Inform the eye surgeon even if treatment ended long ago. After several missed days contact the prescriber to resume the 0.4-mg regimen.

The source label describes Flomax 0.4-mg hard gelatin capsules with an olive-green cap and orange body, marked “Flomax 0.4 mg” and “BI 58.” The source manufacturer package is a 100-capsule bottle, NDC 0024-5837-01. The retrieved DailyMed record is a RedPharm repackaged label with its own NDC; its packaging should not be conflated with that source bottle. Other generic appearances vary.

The selected U.S. Flomax product is a 0.4-mg capsule; a 0.8-mg regimen uses two capsules. Do not treat different formulations or non-U.S. product strengths as interchangeable without checking their specific label.
Store at 25°C (77°F); excursions of 15–30°C (59–86°F) are permitted. Keep out of children’s reach and preserve capsules intact until use.
