assertions: Eliquis reduces stroke/systemic embolism risk in adult nonvalvular AF; prevents DVT after adult hip or knee replacement; treats adult DVT and PE; and reduces recurrent DVT/PE risk after initial treatment. These uses have separate dosing and treatment-duration requirements.

Treatment of VTE and reduction of recurrence are approved from birth after at least 5 days of initial anticoagulant therapy. Pediatric use below 2.6 kg is not recommended because it was not studied. The pediatric approval does not extend adult AF or orthopedic-prophylaxis regimens to children.

The label does not recommend apixaban for prosthetic heart valves or triple-positive antiphospholipid syndrome. It is not an alternative to unfractionated heparin for initial PE treatment with hemodynamic instability or anticipated thrombolysis/embolectomy.
Take orally twice daily. Food does not materially affect bioavailability. Select the regimen by indication.

rows: 5 mg twice daily; 2.5 mg twice daily only when ≥2 apply: age ≥80 years, weight ≤60 kg, serum creatinine ≥1.5 mg/dL
2.5 mg twice daily, starting 12–24 hours after surgery; 35 days after hip or 12 days after knee replacement
10 mg twice daily for the first 7 days, then 5 mg twice daily
2.5 mg twice daily after at least 6 months of DVT / PE treatment

assertions: Begin the apixaban regimen after at least 5 days of initial anticoagulation. The day numbers in this table refer to apixaban treatment, not the preceding therapy. Reassess the weight tier as the child grows and individualize total duration. All entries below are twice-daily doses.

Adults and children ≥35 kg may use 2.5 or 5 mg tablets. They can be crushed into water, D5W or apple juice, or mixed with applesauce and promptly given. For a 12 French NG tube, suspend crushed tablets in 60 mL water or D5W and flush afterward with 20 mL. Stability of these crushed-tablet preparations is up to 4 hours; do not substitute this method for the pediatric packet/capsule instructions.

For 2.6 to <4 kg use the 0.15 mg Sprinkle capsules: open and mix the entire prescribed contents with water or infant formula; do not swallow the capsule. For 4 to <35 kg use 0.5 mg tablets supplied in packets; mix with water, formula, apple juice or applesauce, not swallowed whole. Liquid mixtures must be administered within 2 hours; applesauce mixtures immediately. Use the exact IFU volumes, oral syringe and rinse steps to deliver the full dose. The 0.5 mg packet-tablet liquid mixture has specified NG/G-tube options; obtain tube-size and preparation instructions rather than extrapolating to Sprinkle capsules.

Take a missed dose as soon as possible on the same day and resume twice-daily dosing; never double. For a child vomiting or spitting up within 30 minutes, repeat the dose; after more than 30 minutes, do not repeat and give the next scheduled dose. Repeated vomiting requires clinician advice.

The label calls for at least 48 hours of interruption before procedures with moderate/high bleeding risk, or at least 24 hours for low-risk procedures with readily controlled bleeding. Bridging during this short interruption is generally unnecessary; restart once adequate hemostasis is established. Neuraxial procedures require a separate anesthesia plan; these general surgical intervals are not a complete neuraxial protocol.

From warfarin, start apixaban when INR is below 2.0. Apixaban affects INR during the reverse transition; one labeled approach starts both warfarin and a parenteral anticoagulant when the next apixaban dose would be due, stopping the parenteral drug when INR is acceptable. For transitions with other oral/parenteral anticoagulants, start the replacement at the next scheduled dose time. Use a supervised plan to avoid gaps or unintended overlap.

Serious or fatal bleeding can occur; stop apixaban for active pathological hemorrhage and assess promptly. Other antithrombotics, NSAIDs and SSRIs/SNRIs can increase bleeding risk. Premature cessation without alternative anticoagulation increases thrombotic risk.

Neuraxial hematoma may cause permanent paralysis. The label specifies no catheter removal earlier than 24 hours after the last dose, no next dose earlier than 5 hours after removal, and a 48-hour delay after traumatic puncture. These are label precautions, not a complete anesthesia protocol; optimal timing is not established and pediatric catheter timing has no supporting data. New leg weakness/numbness or bowel/bladder dysfunction needs urgent evaluation.

Active pathological bleeding and severe hypersensitivity to apixaban or the product are contraindications. Renal/hepatic and indication-specific restrictions require additional review even when they are not formal contraindications.

sourceAudit.card: Boxed warning · Thrombosis and spinal hematoma
assertions: The boxed warning addresses increased thrombosis after premature discontinuation and spinal/epidural hematoma with neuraxial anesthesia or spinal puncture. Risk rises with indwelling catheters, other hemostasis-altering drugs, traumatic/repeated puncture and spinal deformity or surgery. Plan interruption and observe neurologic status.

Bleeding is the principal adult adverse reaction. Pediatric trial events commonly included headache, vomiting and excessive menstrual bleeding. Investigate blood loss, anemia or abnormal uterine bleeding rather than dismissing these as routine nuisance effects.

sourceAudit.card: Combined P-gp and strong CYP3A4 inhibitors
assertions: For adults taking 5 or 10 mg twice daily, reduce the apixaban dose by 50% with combined P-gp/strong CYP3A4 inhibitors such as ketoconazole, itraconazole or ritonavir. Avoid these combinations when already taking 2.5 mg twice daily. Pediatric coadministration has not been studied; do not invent an adult-style weight-based adjustment. The label specifically states that clarithromycin does not require adjustment on pharmacokinetic grounds.

Avoid combined strong CYP3A4/P-gp inducers such as rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin and St. John’s wort: lower exposure can increase stroke or thrombosis risk. Antiplatelets, anticoagulants, thrombolytics, chronic NSAIDs and SSRIs/SNRIs increase bleeding risk and need an explicit benefit/risk review.

For AF, use the two-of-three reduction criteria rather than serum creatinine alone. For adult surgical prophylaxis and VTE, the label recommends no renal dose adjustment, including ESRD on dialysis; however, clinical studies excluded dialysis and CrCl below 15 mL/min, so those recommendations rely on PK/PD evidence. AF outcome equivalence on dialysis remains unknown.

Apixaban is not recommended at eGFR below 30 mL/min/1.73 m² for age ≥2 years. For younger children, apply the label’s age-specific renal adequacy criteria; these are not the adult AF rule. The label table gives thresholds for both sexes: at 1 week, eGFR <8; at 2–8 weeks, <12; and after 8 weeks to <2 years, <22 mL/min/1.73 m². Specialist assessment is needed for neonatal ages not explicitly covered in that table.

Child-Pugh A needs no adjustment. No dosing recommendation can be provided for Child-Pugh B because of coagulation abnormalities and limited experience. Use is not recommended in Child-Pugh C; pediatric hepatic impairment has not been studied.

Use in pregnancy is not recommended; human data are limited and maternal/fetal bleeding is a concern. Discuss pregnancy plans and abnormal uterine bleeding. As delivery approaches, a shorter-acting anticoagulant may be considered under a coordinated obstetric/anticoagulation plan.

sources.sections: Summary of Use during Lactation; Drug Levels

assertions: Breastfeeding is not recommended on apixaban. Although the product label retains an older absence-of-human-data statement, current LactMed documents substantial milk transfer and prefers an alternative, especially for newborn/preterm infants. Older adults still need the indication-specific dose criteria and assessment of organ function and interacting therapy.

Apixaban inhibits free and clot-bound factor Xa and prothrombinase activity without requiring antithrombin. PT/INR/aPTT changes at therapeutic doses are small and variable, making these tests unsuitable for routine assessment of anticoagulant effect. Specialized assays require a clinical question and local interpretation.

Oral bioavailability is about 50%, with peaks at 3–4 hours. Protein binding is about 87% and adult half-life about 12 hours. CYP3A4 is the main metabolic pathway; renal excretion contributes about 27% of total clearance, with intestinal/biliary elimination also contributing. The pediatric label reports a peak around 2 hours after a single dose; adult PK values must not replace pediatric weight-tier dosing.

Review the indication, dose, weight when relevant, renal/hepatic status, bleeding history and full medicine list. Follow bleeding or anemia symptoms and new interacting drugs. Do not stop without a plan; report blood in urine/stool, prolonged bleeding, faintness or neurologic symptoms. Tell dentists and procedural teams about treatment. Caregivers need hands-on preparation training and weight-tier review.

sourceAudit.card: Major bleeding and current reversal context
assertions: Anticoagulant effects can persist for at least 24 hours after a dose. Vitamin K and protamine do not reverse apixaban; dialysis has little effect. The current label allows consideration of PCC-based management but does not establish its clinical efficacy. FDA found Andexxa’s risks outweighed benefits and reported the end of U.S. sales on December 22, 2025; do not rely on older labels describing routine availability. Emergency specialists should use the current local protocol.

Suspected overdose or accidental ingestion requires urgent poison-center/medical assessment. Activated charcoal can reduce absorption in selected circumstances; this is a supervised toxicology decision, not a home treatment. Continue bleeding surveillance and supportive management.

Eliquis 5 mg tablets are pink, oval and biconvex with 894 / 5 imprints. Example bottle of 60: NDC 0003-0894-21. Pediatric packets and Sprinkle capsules have different strengths and preparation requirements; appearance alone does not establish the correct dose.

Adult/≥35 kg tablets contain 2.5 or 5 mg. Pediatric 0.5 mg tablets for suspension are supplied as packets containing 1, 3 or 4 tablets, corresponding to 0.5, 1.5 or 2 mg per packet. Sprinkle capsules contain 0.15 mg powder and are opened for suspension. Verify both tablet count and packet total.

Store Eliquis and Sprinkle at 20–25°C with excursions to 15–30°C. Follow formulation-specific mixture timing: pediatric liquids within 2 hours, applesauce mixtures immediately, and crushed 2.5/5 mg preparations up to 4 hours. Keep medicines away from children and use prescribed oral dosing equipment.

assertions: Simvastatin reduces mortality and coronary/cerebrovascular events and revascularization risk in defined high-risk adults with coronary, cerebrovascular or peripheral vascular disease and/or diabetes. It is used with diet for primary hyperlipidemia, HeFH, primary dysbetalipoproteinemia and hypertriglyceridemia; adult HoFH use is adjunctive to other LDL-lowering therapies.

The pediatric approval is for LDL reduction with diet in HeFH from age 10 years. Other pediatric lipid disorders and younger ages are not established uses. Current AHA/ACC guidance combines risk assessment, LDL/non-HDL goals and percentage reduction; if high-intensity therapy is required or goals remain unmet at 40 mg, the label directs an alternative LDL-lowering treatment.

Take orally once daily in the evening. Adults: the recommended range is 20–40 mg daily. HeFH from age 10: 10–40 mg daily. Reassess LDL-C as early as 4 weeks after initiation and adjust according to response, tolerance and interaction limits. A missed dose may be taken as soon as possible; do not double the next dose.

The usual recommended maximum is 40 mg daily. An 80 mg regimen is reserved for patients already taking 80 mg chronically, such as for at least 12 months, without muscle toxicity; do not start or titrate a patient to 80 mg. If an interacting drug is needed in someone on 80 mg, select another statin. Zocor no longer markets its 80 mg strength.

For severe renal impairment with creatinine clearance 15–29 mL/min, start at 5 mg once daily. Zocor’s 5 mg strength is no longer marketed, so select an appropriate alternative simvastatin tablet product. Mild/moderate renal impairment has no recommended dose adjustment, but all renal impairment increases muscle-toxicity risk. The cited dosing section does not establish a routine regimen for CrCl below 15.

Apply the exact co-medication cap even when the usual adult dose would be higher. Lomitapide’s legacy 40 mg exception is restricted to patients previously tolerating chronic 80 mg; it is not a new-start regimen.

rows: Reduce by 50%; maximum 20 mg daily, or restricted legacy 40 mg exception
Strong CYP3A4 inhibitor; cyclosporine; danazol; gemfibrozil

assertions: The reviewed regimens refer to oral tablets. Marketed Zocor strengths are 10, 20 and 40 mg; generic labels also describe 5 and 80 mg tablets. Strength availability does not override dose restrictions. Liquid or combination products require their own label and administration/storage instructions.

Myopathy and rhabdomyolysis can cause kidney injury or death. Risk increases with higher doses, age ≥65, uncontrolled hypothyroidism, renal impairment and interacting medicines. Stop for suspected myopathy or markedly elevated CK. Serious illness with high rhabdomyolysis-related renal risk, such as sepsis, shock or major trauma, may require temporary cessation.

Persistent proximal weakness and elevated CK despite stopping can indicate immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy; stop and obtain specialist assessment. Consider baseline liver enzymes and repeat when clinically indicated; promptly stop for serious symptomatic liver injury, jaundice or hyperbilirubinemia. HbA1c/glucose can rise; maintain lifestyle and metabolic follow-up.

Strong CYP3A4 inhibitor coadministration, cyclosporine, danazol or gemfibrozil, acute liver failure/decompensated cirrhosis, and hypersensitivity to simvastatin or ingredients are contraindications. Pregnancy is no longer an absolute U.S. statin contraindication; the separate pregnancy risk assessment remains essential.
The reviewed simvastatin tablet labels do not carry an FDA boxed warning. This does not diminish the important muscle, interaction and hepatic precautions, including the restriction on 80 mg dosing.

Common reported trial events include headache, abdominal discomfort, constipation and nausea; upper respiratory infection was also commonly recorded. Serious postmarketing events include hepatic failure, immune-mediated myopathy and severe hypersensitivity. New or worsening myasthenia gravis and generally reversible cognitive symptoms have also been reported; spontaneous reports do not establish frequency or causation.

Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors include selected azoles (itraconazole, ketoconazole, posaconazole, voriconazole), macrolides (erythromycin, clarithromycin), boosted protease-inhibitor/cobicistat products and nefazodone. Suspend simvastatin for an unavoidable short course of a strong inhibitor. Cyclosporine, danazol and gemfibrozil are also contraindicated. Confirm the exact antiviral regimen rather than assuming every antiviral has the same interaction.

Observe the cardiac-drug and lomitapide caps above. Review temporary suspension during daptomycin treatment. Other fibrates, colchicine and lipid-modifying niacin doses (≥1 g/day) need benefit/risk review and muscle surveillance. Simvastatin with lipid-modifying niacin is not recommended in Chinese patients. Avoid grapefruit juice.

Obtain INR before initiating simvastatin with a coumarin anticoagulant, then check sufficiently often after starting, dose changes or discontinuation until stable. Simvastatin can increase digoxin concentrations; monitor levels when simvastatin is initiated.

sources.sections: What should healthcare professionals do?; Data summary

assertions: Discontinue when pregnancy is recognized in most patients. FDA removed the blanket statin pregnancy contraindication in 2021 to permit individualized decisions for very high-risk patients, including HoFH or established cardiovascular disease. Available observational data do not show a clear increase in major malformations after adjustment, but miscarriage risk is uncertain and fetal harm remains possible. Discuss any exceptional continuation with specialists.

Breastfeeding is not recommended while taking simvastatin because of potential effects on infant cholesterol metabolism and limited infant safety evidence. Discuss temporarily withholding lipid treatment or an alternative feeding plan when continued therapy is necessary.

HeFH approval starts at age 10; trial girls were at least one year post-menarche. Do not impose an unverified approval for other pediatric lipid disorders or doses above 40 mg. Older adults have greater myopathy risk; choose doses cautiously and assess concomitant disease, renal function and medicines.

Monitor renal impairment for muscle toxicity and use the severe-renal starting-dose rule. Acute liver failure or decompensated cirrhosis is contraindicated; substantial alcohol use or liver history warrants assessment. The label reports greater myopathy risk in Chinese patients, particularly with niacin combinations; monitor and avoid the stated combination.

Simvastatin is hydrolyzed to simvastatin acid, which inhibits HMG-CoA reductase. Increased hepatic LDL-receptor expression promotes LDL uptake and lowers circulating LDL-C. Maximal LDL reduction is usually reached by about 4 weeks.

Extensive hepatic first-pass extraction leaves low systemic availability (below 5%). Simvastatin and its active acid are about 95% protein bound. CYP3A4 metabolism and OATP1B1 transport help explain exposure interactions. Active/total inhibitor peaks occur around 1.3–2.4 hours; labeled radiolabel recovery is mainly fecal, with a smaller urinary component.

Assess baseline lipid status, cardiovascular risk, relevant organ function, muscle history, hypothyroidism and interacting medicines. Consider liver enzymes before therapy and thereafter for clinical indications. Follow LDL response from about 4 weeks onward. Investigate symptoms with CK and related testing as clinically appropriate; avoid turning the label into a universal schedule for asymptomatic CK testing.

The 2026 AHA/ACC guideline replaces the 2018 cholesterol guideline and uses PREVENT-ASCVD for relevant primary-prevention risk assessment, with individualized lipid goals and additional risk information. This monograph does not reproduce the full eligibility algorithm; select treatment intensity and alternatives with the applicable guideline and patient-specific risk.

Take in the evening, avoid grapefruit juice and check before starting any new drug or supplement. Report unexplained muscle pain/weakness, especially with fever or malaise, and jaundice or dark urine. Notify the clinician about pregnancy plans or a recognized pregnancy. Suspected overdose requires poison-center advice; no specific simvastatin antidote is known.
Zocor 20 mg is a tan, oval tablet marked MSD 740 on one side, plain on the other. Example bottle of 30: NDC 78206-181-01. It is manufactured for Organon; generic tablet appearance and NDC differ.

Zocor currently markets 10, 20 and 40 mg tablets; its 5 and 80 mg strengths are no longer marketed. The reviewed generic label describes 5, 10, 20, 40 and 80 mg tablet strengths. The presence of an 80 mg strength is not permission to initiate it. This page does not supply liquid or combination-product instructions.

For the reviewed Zocor product, store between 5°C and 30°C. Generic tablet storage instructions can differ; follow the dispensed label and keep away from children. Do not apply this tablet storage range to a separately formulated oral suspension.

Toujeo explicitly indicates diabetes in adults and children ≥6 years. Basaglar specifically indicates adult/pediatric type 1 diabetes and adult type 2 diabetes; pediatric type 2 use and type 1 use below 6 are not established. Do not assign one universal minimum age to every product.

All selected products are basal insulin and are not recommended for treating diabetic ketoacidosis. In type 1 diabetes, combine with short-/rapid-acting premeal insulin. This profile excludes fixed insulin glargine/lixisenatide combinations and individualized emergency insulin protocols.
These starting regimens require individual assessment; they are not a total insulin prescription.

Adjust no more often than every 3–4 days. Full glucose-lowering effect may take 5 days; monitor daily at initiation.

paragraphs: Increase glucose checks during changes and early follow-up; other diabetes medicines may also need adjustment.

paragraphs: Inject once daily at the same time under the skin of abdomen, thigh or upper arm. Rotate sites; avoid pits, thickened skin or amyloid lumps. Use only clear, colorless solution. Do not mix, dilute, use in a pump, or administer intravenously. A pen displays actual units; no concentration calculation is needed. Never withdraw from a pen with a syringe.

900 units/3 mL; 2-unit increments, up to 160 units/injection; recommended if needing ≥20 units/day. Odd-unit conversion between pens requires clinician-directed ±1 unit.
1-unit increments. Basaglar, Rezvoglar, Lantus SoloStar and Semglee pen instructions limit a single injection to 80 units.

sourceAudit.card: Renal, hepatic and changing insulin needs

paragraphs: No fixed renal/hepatic adjustment is provided. Monitor more often and individualize units with changes in renal/hepatic function, meals, activity, acute illness or other medicines. Do not apply an arbitrary dose ceiling: device limits describe one injection rather than a maximum daily prescription.

items: Severe hypoglycemia can cause seizure, coma or death. Renal/hepatic impairment, missed meals, activity changes and interacting medicines increase risk; reduced warning symptoms require more frequent checks.
Never share pens, syringes or needles, even with a new needle. Check product and concentration every injection; never use a syringe to extract pen contents.
Changes in brand, concentration, injection site or technique require supervision and extra glucose monitoring. Moving from a repeatedly used abnormal site to healthy skin can cause hypoglycemia.
Insulin moves potassium into cells; monitor potassium in patients at risk. Severe low potassium can cause arrhythmia or paralysis.
Anaphylaxis requires stopping the product and emergency treatment. TZDs with insulin can cause fluid retention or worsen heart failure; review swelling, dyspnea or sudden weight gain.

paragraphs: Do not administer during an episode of hypoglycemia or with hypersensitivity to insulin glargine/the selected product’s ingredients.
The selected U.S. labels have no boxed warning. Severe hypoglycemia, medication errors, anaphylaxis, hypokalemia and infection from sharing devices remain important labeled risks.

Hypoglycemia, weight gain, edema, injection-site reactions, lipodystrophy and localized cutaneous amyloidosis are reported. Immunogenicity occurs; antibody tests and trial adverse-event rates are not directly comparable across products. Excess insulin can cause prolonged/recurrent hypoglycemia and hypokalemia. Treat mild lows with oral carbohydrate if able to swallow; severe symptoms need emergency glucagon or IV glucose and continued observation. Do not give food/drink to an unconscious person.

rows: Other glucose-lowering agents; ACE inhibitors/ARBs, salicylates, fluoxetine, selected antibiotics
Hypoglycemia risk may rise; more glucose checks and an insulin reduction may be needed.
Corticosteroids, atypical antipsychotics, sympathomimetics, thyroid hormones, selected hormones/diuretics
Glucose-lowering effect may decline; monitor and adjust insulin if needed.
Glucose response may increase or decrease; pentamidine can cause lows followed by highs. Monitor closely.
May mask hypoglycemia symptoms; rely on more frequent glucose checks.
Monitor fluid retention/heart failure; consider TZD reduction or discontinuation if heart failure develops.

paragraphs: Published glargine pregnancy studies have not established a clear association with adverse developmental outcomes; observational limitations remain. Poor glycemic control poses maternal/fetal risks, and both low and high glucose require attention. Human milk data are absent or limited; endogenous insulin is in milk. Balance maternal treatment and breastfeeding benefits with potential infant effects and monitor changing insulin needs.

Toujeo is labeled ≥6 years; not established below 6. Basaglar pediatric type 1 evidence is ages 6–15; below 6 and pediatric type 2 are not established. Lantus, Semglee and Rezvoglar have broad pediatric diabetes indication wording supported by type 1 ages 6–15 plus adult studies; their selected labels do not state the same explicit minimum as Toujeo. Pediatric type 1 trial severe hypoglycemia was more frequent than in adult trials; specialist dosing and caregiver training are essential.

Use conservative initiation and increments in older adults, where lows may be harder to recognize. Kidney/hepatic effects on glargine pharmacokinetics have not been directly studied adequately; frequent glucose checks and dose adjustment may be necessary. No eGFR-based fixed unit adjustment is supplied.

Insulin promotes peripheral glucose uptake and suppresses hepatic glucose output. It also inhibits lipolysis/proteolysis and promotes protein synthesis. Glargine’s subcutaneous absorption provides prolonged basal activity.
Time-action profiles vary within and between patients; do not promise a fixed duration for every injection.
facts: Relatively constant concentrations with no pronounced peak versus NPH over 24 hours. Lantus clamp median effect was 24 hours; range included 10.8 to >24 hours.
Onset develops over approximately 6 hours in single-dose clamp studies; steady-state concentrations reached by at least 5 days. Unit-for-unit glucose-lowering effect differs from U-100.
Subcutaneous/circulating active metabolites M1 and M2 have insulin-like activity.
Pen units do not require volume conversion; pharmacologic differences still require product-specific switching and titration.

items: Monitor glucose according to the individualized plan; increase checks during brand/concentration changes, illness, meals/activity changes or impaired low-glucose awareness.
Review hypoglycemia episodes, injection sites, technique, adherence and storage. Check glycemic progress and whether basal/mealtime balance remains appropriate.
Check potassium in at-risk patients; follow weight, edema and heart failure symptoms with TZDs.
Review kidney/hepatic function changes and interacting drugs; reassess dose under medical supervision.
Read the exact device instructions, prime as directed, use a new needle each time and remove it after injection. Confirm product, concentration and prescribed units.
Never share any pen or needle; do not transfer insulin from a pen to a syringe. Use the correct U-100 syringe only for a U-100 vial.
Carry a low-glucose treatment plan and teach caregivers emergency glucagon use. Discuss safe driving and alcohol; lows may recur because this insulin lasts a long time.
Rotate healthy injection sites; keep a clinician-directed plan for missed doses/illness. Do not stop necessary basal insulin or double a dose without guidance.

sources.note: Full public manufacturer label and patient instructions; SPL version 31, effective 20260130. Product-specific directions reviewed October 1, 2026.

paragraphs: Adults: reduces cardiovascular death/HF hospitalization in heart failure; reduces sustained eGFR decline, end-stage kidney disease, cardiovascular death and hospitalization in CKD at risk of progression; reduces cardiovascular death in type 2 diabetes with established cardiovascular disease. With diet/exercise, improves type 2 diabetes glycemic control in adults and children ≥10 years. HF and CKD indication wording does not require diabetes.

Not recommended for type 1 diabetes glycemic control due to ketoacidosis risk, or type 2 glycemic control at eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m² because glucose lowering is likely ineffective. CKD treatment is not recommended in polycystic kidney disease or with current/recent IV immunosuppression or >45 mg prednisone-equivalent for kidney disease. These limitations are distinct from the formal allergy contraindication.
Take once daily in the morning, with or without food.

rows: Adult type 2 diabetes with established cardiovascular disease · cardiovascular death reduction
Adult / pediatric ≥10 type 2 diabetes glycemic control
10 mg once daily; may increase to 25 mg if tolerated and additional glucose lowering is needed.
Check renal function and volume status; correct volume depletion.

paragraphs: Withhold at least 3 days, if possible, before surgery or procedures involving prolonged fasting. Resume when clinically stable and oral intake has resumed. Also consider temporary interruption during illnesses or situations predisposing to ketoacidosis. For a missed dose, take when remembered unless almost time for the next; skip rather than double.

Glycemic use is not recommended below eGFR 30 mL/min/1.73 m². HF trials enrolled eGFR ≥20; CKD trial eGFR 20–90. Trials did not enroll eGFR <20 or patients already on dialysis, so do not infer an initiation regimen there. Enrolled patients were not required to stop solely for later decline below 20 or starting dialysis; reassess clinically. Hepatic impairment is permitted without a labeled dose change.

items: Ketoacidosis may be fatal and occur at glucose <250 mg/dL. Risk rises with missed/reduced insulin, pancreatic disease, acute illness, fasting/ketogenic diet, surgery, dehydration or heavy alcohol. Stop, evaluate ketones/acidosis promptly and treat; confirm resolution before restarting.
Glucosuria can persist 3 days and ketoacidosis/glucosuria has sometimes lasted >6 days to 2 weeks after stopping. A normal-looking glucose reading does not rule it out.
Volume depletion, hypotension and acute kidney injury can occur, especially with older age, eGFR <60 or loop diuretics. Correct depletion before use and monitor renal function/symptoms.

UTI/genital infection can progress to urosepsis, pyelonephritis or Fournier gangrene in patients with or without diabetes. Perineal pain/swelling/redness plus fever/malaise needs immediate evaluation; stop if Fournier gangrene is suspected and treat urgently.
Hypoglycemia increases with insulin/sulfonylureas in adults; children ≥10 have increased risk even without insulin. Review concomitant doses without unnecessary insulin omission.
Monitor new foot pain, sores, ulcers or infection and provide preventive foot care; lower-limb amputation is a labeled precaution. Stop for serious hypersensitivity and treat promptly.

paragraphs: Hypersensitivity to empagliflozin or any Jardiance ingredient; serious reactions including angioedema have occurred. Renal/indication limitations and ketoacidosis risks are discussed separately.
The selected current Jardiance label has no boxed warning. Ketoacidosis, severe genitourinary infection, volume depletion and other serious risks remain labeled precautions.

Common reported reactions include urinary tract infection and female genital mycotic infection; increased urination, thirst, male genital infection and nausea also occur. Hypoglycemia risk depends on population/co-therapy. Serious risks are summarized above; postmarketing reports cannot establish incidence. For overdose seek medical/Poison Help guidance (U.S. 1-800-222-1222); removal by hemodialysis is unstudied.

rows: Assess/correct volume depletion and monitor volume status/renal function.
May need lower co-therapy dose to reduce hypoglycemia; excessive insulin reduction can precipitate ketoacidosis.
SGLT2 inhibitors may lower serum lithium; check levels more frequently at initiation/dose changes.
Glucosuria is expected and 1,5-AG is unreliable; use alternative glycemic monitoring.

paragraphs: Not recommended in the second/third trimesters because animal data raise fetal kidney-development concerns; limited human data cannot define congenital/miscarriage risk. Poorly controlled diabetes also poses risk; review alternatives with the clinician. Breastfeeding is not recommended because of potential postnatal kidney effects; human milk data are limited.

Type 2 diabetes glycemic control is established at age ≥10; younger children and pediatric outcome indications are not established. Children have higher hypoglycemia risk regardless of insulin use. Older adults, especially ≥75 in glucose-control trials, had more volume-depletion/UTI reactions; assess hydration and renal function.

Glucose lowering declines with worsening kidney function and renal/volume/UTI adverse risks rise. Distinguish eGFR <30 glycemic limitation from HF/CKD trials at ≥20. No trial enrollment below 20 or on dialysis establishes initiation there. Hepatic impairment is allowed; no dose adjustment is specified.

Empagliflozin blocks proximal renal SGLT2 glucose reabsorption, increasing urinary glucose loss. Reduced sodium reabsorption increases distal sodium delivery and may contribute to tubuloglomerular feedback and other cardiovascular/renal effects. Glucosuria typically approaches baseline about 3 days after stopping, though prolonged postmarketing cases occur.

facts: Peak approximately 1.5 hours after oral dosing; food effect is not clinically important.
Mainly glucuronidation; no major plasma metabolite, with each major conjugate <10% of drug-related material.
Apparent terminal half-life about 12.4 hours; radiolabeled material recovered in urine (~54%) and feces (~41%).

items: Check renal function and volume status before starting and as clinically indicated; monitor dehydration, dizziness and changes after diuretics.
Follow glucose/HbA1c as appropriate; educate all patients about lows and use closer observation in children or insulin/sulfonylurea users.
Assess ketones when clinical risk/symptoms warrant; evaluate acidosis even with glucose <250 mg/dL.
Review urinary/genital infection symptoms, feet/ulcers and lithium levels when relevant.
Take the prescribed tablet each morning; do not double missed doses. Arrange stopping ≥3 days before surgery/prolonged fasting and clinician-directed restart.
Report inability to eat/drink, vomiting or acute illness; agree on fluid advice appropriate to HF/CKD rather than forcing an arbitrary fluid intake.
Stop and seek urgent care for ketoacidosis symptoms; genital/perineal pain, redness or swelling with fever/malaise also needs immediate care.
Report urinary infection, genital yeast symptoms, new foot sores or pain, and pregnancy. Discuss breastfeeding alternatives.

facts: Pale yellow, round, biconvex/beveled · S 10 / company symbol

paragraphs: Standalone Jardiance tablets: 10 mg round (S 10) and 25 mg oval (S 25), pale yellow and film-coated. Bottles and institutional blister cards are described in the label. Empagliflozin combinations such as metformin/linagliptin products are outside this reference.
Store at 20–25°C; permitted excursions 15–30°C. Dispense in a well-closed container and keep out of children’s reach. Read the Medication Guide.

claims: Oral and selected injection labels cover adult/pediatric edema with heart failure, cirrhosis or renal disease including nephrotic syndrome. Oral products also cover adult hypertension; injection is adjunctive therapy for acute pulmonary edema.

The AHA/ACC/HFSA guideline recommends diuretics for fluid retention to relieve congestion and prevent worsening heart failure. Reserve addition of a thiazide to a loop diuretic for inadequate response to moderate/high loop doses, to limit electrolyte abnormalities.
Edema
20–80 mg once initially; repeat or increase by 20–40 mg no sooner than 6–8 hours. Maintenance once/twice daily. Severe edema may require carefully supervised titration up to 600 mg/day.
Hypertension
80 mg/day initially, usually 40 mg twice daily; adjust to BP response and review other antihypertensives.

Edema: 20–40 mg IV/IM initially; IV over 1–2 minutes. Repeat/increase by 20 mg no sooner than 2 hours, then once/twice daily as individualized. Acute pulmonary edema: 40 mg IV over 1–2 minutes; if inadequate after 1 hour, 80 mg IV over 1–2 minutes. Continuous infusion must not exceed 4 mg/min; high-dose therapy requires controlled infusion.

Oral edema: 2 mg/kg once initially; increase 1–2 mg/kg no sooner than 6–8 hours. IV/IM: 1 mg/kg initially over 1–2 minutes; increase 1 mg/kg no sooner than 2 hours. Both labels advise against doses above 6 mg/kg. Selected injection limits premature infants to 1 mg/kg/day.

Anuria is contraindicated. Stop for increasing azotemia plus oliguria in progressive severe renal disease. Cirrhosis/ascites warrants hospital initiation and careful titration; correct hepatic coma/electrolyte depletion first. Oral solutions are 8 or 10 mg/mL; verify concentration and measuring device. No automatic oral-to-IV conversion is supplied here.

Dehydration, hypotension, electrolyte depletion and metabolic abnormalities may be severe. Rapid injection, renal impairment, excessive doses, low albumin and ototoxic drugs increase hearing risk. Watch for urinary retention. Assess sulfonamide allergy history, lupus, glucose and gout risks.
Anuria or prior hypersensitivity to furosemide.

Selected oral labels prominently warn of profound diuresis and water/electrolyte depletion requiring medical supervision. The selected modern injection PI has no boxed warning; its serious volume/electrolyte and hearing warnings still apply.

Dizziness, orthostasis, GI upset, cramps and photosensitivity occur. Serious reports include hearing loss, severe allergy/skin reactions, blood disorders and renal injury. Overdose requires urgent supportive fluid/electrolyte correction and BP monitoring; dialysis does not speed elimination.
Avoid lithium; avoid ethacrynic acid and aminoglycosides except life-threatening indications.
Cisplatin/nephrotoxic drugs require renal/hearing review.
ACE inhibitors/ARBs and other antihypertensives: monitor BP/renal function; doses may need reduction.
NSAIDs/phenytoin may reduce response. Methotrexate/tubularly secreted drugs can increase toxicity.
Potassium-depleting medicines increase risk; hypokalemia enhances digoxin toxicity.
Separate oral tablets and sucralfate by at least 2 hours.
Review high-dose salicylates, cyclosporine, chloral hydrate and perioperative muscle relaxants against the full label.

Use requires individualized maternal/fetal assessment. The newer injection PI reports no demonstrated major-malformation signal from available observational data; this does not establish absence of risk. Furosemide enters milk and significant diuresis may impair supply.

Premature infants have hearing, nephrocalcinosis and nephrolithiasis risks; assess renal function/ultrasound as labeled. Oral labeling notes possible persistent ductus risk early in premature life. Older adults often need lower starting doses and renal assessment.
Inhibits renal sodium/chloride reabsorption, particularly in the loop of Henle, producing diuresis.
Oral effect
Onset within 1 hour; duration 6–8 hours.
IV effect
Onset within 5 minutes; duration approximately 2 hours.
Disposition
Highly albumin-bound; predominantly urinary elimination.
Half-life
Approximately 2 hours; patient factors alter clearance.
Assess BP, hydration, urine output and edema response.
Check sodium/potassium, CO₂, BUN/creatinine; assess magnesium/calcium, glucose and uric acid as appropriate.
Check hearing symptoms and urinary retention.
Infant renal function/ultrasound and high-dose treatment require additional surveillance.

Rise slowly. Report fainting, cramps, marked thirst, reduced urine or hearing changes. Follow the prescribed fluid/potassium plan and sun protection. Measure liquid with the supplied calibrated device; verify strength every refill.

7.5 mg orally once daily; may increase to 15 mg/day.

5 mg once daily; may increase to 10 mg/day.
Xifyrm IV; historical Anjeso
30 mg once daily by IV bolus over 15 seconds. Hydrate first; assess need for short-acting non-NSAID rescue.

Tablets: 7.5 mg once daily only at≥60 kg; do not use below 60 kg. Suspension: age≥2, 0.125 mg/kg once daily, max 7.5 mg; 1.5 mg/mL concentration. Higher doses gave no additional benefit. Capsule and IV pediatric safety/effectiveness are unestablished.

Standard oral products: severe renal impairment not recommended; dialysis maximum 7.5 mg/day for tablet/suspension versus 5 mg/day for 5/10 mg capsules. IV products: not recommended with moderate/severe renal insufficiency; contraindicated when such patients risk renal failure from volume depletion. Mild/moderate hepatic impairment generally needs no oral adjustment; severe disease is poorly studied and warrants caution/monitoring. IV hepatic data are limited. For IV therapy, consider dose reduction and adverse-effect monitoring in known/suspected poor CYP2C9 metabolizers; the label gives no fixed alternate regimen.

Standard tablets/suspension may be taken with or without food; gently shake suspension and measure accurately. Labels warn against assuming equivalent exposure across oral formulations. The suspension label specifically permits corresponding 7.5/15 mg standard-tablet substitution, alongside a broader non-interchangeability warning; prescriber/pharmacist must verify the exact switch. 5/10 mg capsules are not equivalent to standard tablets.

Avoid after recent MI or with severe heart failure unless benefit outweighs risk. Monitor BP, edema, renal function and potassium; correct dehydration first. Stop for suspected liver injury, serious skin reaction or DRESS. NSAIDs can mask infection and cause anemia/bleeding.

Meloxicam/product hypersensitivity, prior serious NSAID skin reaction, aspirin/NSAID-triggered asthma or allergic reactions, and CABG surgery. IV products additionally contraindicate moderate/severe renal insufficiency with volume-depletion renal-failure risk.

sourceAudit.card: Boxed warning · Cardiovascular and gastrointestinal events
claims: Selected products warn of potentially fatal MI/stroke and GI bleeding, ulceration or perforation. Risk may begin early; older adults and prior ulcer/GI-bleeding patients face greater GI risk. CABG use is contraindicated.

Oral effects include dyspepsia, diarrhea, nausea, headache and edema. IV trials commonly reported constipation, increased GGT and anemia. Severe allergy, skin reactions, hepatic/renal injury and blood disorders are reported. Overdose requires urgent supportive care; no specific antidote exists and high protein binding limits dialysis usefulness.
Anticoagulants, aspirin, antiplatelets, SSRIs/SNRIs: monitor bleeding. Analgesic-dose aspirin/other NSAIDs are generally not recommended.
ACE inhibitors/ARBs/beta-blockers: monitor BP; assess renal function/hydration with ACE inhibitors/ARBs.
Diuretics: monitor renal function and diuretic/BP response.
Lithium, methotrexate and cyclosporine: monitor toxicity; capsule label also directs digoxin-level monitoring.

Pemetrexed: coordinate oncology-directed interruption at least 5 days before, treatment day and 2 days after; monitor toxicity at CrCl 45–79 mL/min. Standard-tablet label advises against concomitant use below 45.

Between about 20–30 weeks, use only when necessary at lowest dose/shortest duration; consider amniotic-fluid ultrasound beyond 48 hours and stop for oligohydramnios. Avoid at about 30 weeks onward. NSAIDs may reversibly delay ovulation; consider withdrawal when investigating infertility.

Human milk/infant-effect data are unavailable; individualize breastfeeding decisions. JRA age/weight limits apply by oral form; do not extrapolate to capsules/IV. Older adults face greater GI, CV and renal risk. Xifyrm also describes animal male-fertility findings of uncertain human relevance.
Analgesic/anti-inflammatory activity involves COX-1/COX-2 inhibition; the complete mechanism is not established.

Approximately 99% protein-bound.
Metabolism

Approximately 15–20 hours orally; selected Xifyrm study mean 21 hours.
Clearance
Metabolites excreted in urine/feces; not effectively dialyzable.
Assess pain/function and duration; IV product is not for long-term treatment.
Monitor BP, edema and renal function/potassium in at-risk patients.

Check GI bleeding, skin/allergy and liver-injury symptoms; pregnancy ultrasound as directed.

5/10 mg; separate dose/exposure limits.

Xifyrm 30 mg/mL, 1 mL single-dose vial; historical Anjeso 30 mg/mL.
Outside scope
ODT, other suspensions and combination/local-surgical products have separate labels.

Tablets: 20–25°C, dry, tight container. Selected suspension: 25°C, excursions 15–30°C, tightly closed. Capsules: 20–25°C, original tightly closed bottle for moisture protection. Xifyrm: 20–25°C, carton for light protection; inspect and discard unused vial contents.
A nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug. Standard tablets/suspension, 5/10 mg capsules and IV formulations have distinct indications, doses and population limits.
Chest pain, stroke symptoms, bloody vomit or black stools require urgent care. Stop and seek assessment for serious rash or allergy. Verify the exact formulation before dosing.

validationEvidence.caveat: Local full checks and representative visual inspection passed; production publication not verified.

sources.title: Hydrocodone bitartrate and acetaminophen tablets · Prescribing information
sources.note: PI revised January 2026; Proficient Rx repackaging SPL effective July 1, 2026. Includes 5/325, 7.5/325 and 10/325 dosing; package example is 5/325.
sources.review_method: Full relevant clinical SPL sections read; dosing/product table text checked against the source; current manufacturer PDF concordance checked for tirzepatide.
sources.metadata_note: Repackaging effective date July 2026 differs from clinical PI revision January 2026; all substantive clinical sections including MedicationGuide read.

assertions: The reviewed tablets treat pain severe enough to require an opioid when alternative treatments are ineffective, intolerable or insufficient. Risks of addiction and overdose exist at any dose or duration. This is a pain indication, not a cough indication despite hydrocodone’s pharmacologic antitussive activity.

Individualize treatment using prior analgesic exposure, pain severity and patient risk. Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest appropriate period; many acute pain conditions need only a few days. Repeated prescribing requires reassessment of benefit, function, adverse effects and misuse risk.

Use only the prescribed strength and dose. The reviewed immediate-release label gives the following as-needed starting ranges; choose the lowest dose achieving adequate analgesia and titrate individually. These are daily ceilings, not targets.

sources.sections: Dosage and Administration; Warnings / Hepatotoxicity; Precautions / Maximum Daily Dose of Acetaminophen

assertions: The 8-tablet 5/325 maximum contains 2,600 mg APAP; either 6-tablet higher-strength maximum contains 1,950 mg. Count every prescription and OTC APAP source, and do not take multiple APAP products without clinician review. The label’s 4,000 mg/day total APAP limit never overrides a lower prescribed or combination-tablet maximum. Liver disease or alcohol exposure increases concern and may require a different plan.

sources.sections: Dosage and Administration / Conversion; Medication Guide

assertions: Take orally exactly as prescribed; do not double a missed dose. The reviewed label does not establish a food-effect dosing rule. Opioid conversion must be conservative because potency varies between patients; relative bioavailability versus extended-release hydrocodone is not established. Do not substitute ER hydrocodone or a liquid preparation using this tablet schedule.

sources.sections: Dosage and Administration / Titration; Safe Reduction or Discontinuation; Warnings / Hyperalgesia

assertions: Reevaluate worsening pain before increasing the dose; opioid-induced hyperalgesia can worsen pain with escalation. A physically dependent patient needs an agreed, individualized taper with continued pain and mental-health support, not abrupt discontinuation. The label gives 10–25% or smaller total-daily-dose reductions every 2–4 weeks as an example, with slower changes or pauses when needed; this is not a universal schedule.

Monitor sedation and breathing especially at initiation, dose increases, opioid conversion or interaction changes. Pulmonary disease, frailty, sleep-related breathing disorders and concomitant depressants increase risk. Discuss access to naloxone or another appropriate reversal product; one accidental dose can be fatal to a child.

Reassess addiction, misuse and diversion throughout treatment. Watch for hypotension, adrenal insufficiency, seizures, biliary problems and esophageal dysfunction. Avoid use in circulatory shock, coma or impaired consciousness. New pain or sensitivity with dose increases warrants evaluation for hyperalgesia.

APAP can cause serious hepatic injury, particularly with excess total exposure, alcohol or underlying liver disease. Stop and urgently evaluate severe rash, blistering or allergic symptoms. Avoid abrupt opioid withdrawal in dependent patients.

Significant respiratory depression; acute or severe bronchial asthma without monitoring or resuscitation capability; known or suspected GI obstruction including paralytic ileus; and hypersensitivity to hydrocodone or acetaminophen are contraindications.

sourceAudit.card: Boxed warning: opioid and combination risks
assertions: The boxed warning covers addiction/abuse/misuse; life-threatening respiratory depression; accidental ingestion; benzodiazepine or other CNS-depressant combinations; neonatal opioid withdrawal with prolonged pregnancy exposure; opioid REMS education; potentially fatal CYP3A4 interactions; and acetaminophen hepatotoxicity. The APAP component does not mitigate opioid overdose risk.

Frequently reported effects include light-headedness, dizziness, sedation, nausea and vomiting; constipation and urinary retention also occur. Serious reports include respiratory depression, severe skin or allergic reactions, serotonin syndrome, adrenal insufficiency, androgen deficiency, hyperalgesia, hypoglycemia and esophageal dysfunction. Spontaneous reports do not establish a precise frequency.

Adding a CYP3A4 inhibitor such as a macrolide, azole or ritonavir, or stopping an inducer such as rifampin, carbamazepine or phenytoin, can raise hydrocodone exposure and cause respiratory depression. Consider dose reduction and frequent assessment. Adding an inducer or stopping an inhibitor can reduce effect or cause withdrawal; reassess rather than letting the patient self-escalate. Combined CYP3A4/2D6 inhibition may further increase effects.

sources.sections: Drug Interactions / CNS Depressants; Muscle Relaxants; Medication Guide

assertions: Benzodiazepines, gabapentinoids, other opioids, sedative-hypnotics and alcohol can produce additive sedation, coma and fatal respiratory depression. Reserve necessary combinations for inadequate alternatives, minimize dose/duration and arrange monitoring and reversal access. Muscle relaxants can further suppress respiration. Avoid alcohol.

Serotonergic combinations can cause serotonin syndrome; monitor especially when starting or increasing doses and stop the combination opioid if suspected. Use with MAO inhibitors or within 14 days of stopping one is not recommended. Urgent exceptions require specialist titration and close cardiopulmonary monitoring, not routine outpatient substitution.

sources.sections: Drug Interactions / Mixed Agonists; Anticholinergics; Diuretics; Laboratory Tests

assertions: Mixed agonist/antagonist or partial agonist opioids can reduce analgesia or precipitate withdrawal; any transition needs a planned clinical approach. Anticholinergics increase urinary retention and severe constipation/ileus risk. Opioids may reduce diuretic effect; monitor fluid response and blood pressure. APAP can interfere with urinary 5-HIAA testing.

sources.sections: Drug Interactions / Renal and Hepatic Impairment; Precautions / Laboratory Tests; Warnings / Hepatotoxicity

assertions: Renal or hepatic impairment may raise hydrocodone concentrations. Start low and closely follow sedation and respiratory effects; the label does not provide numerical eGFR or Child-Pugh adjustment tables. Serial renal/liver tests are advised for severe disease. Liver risk from APAP must also be considered when choosing the combination.

sources.sections: Drug Interactions / Pediatric and Geriatric Use; Warnings

assertions: Safety and effectiveness of these tablets in pediatric patients are not established; do not copy pediatric APAP doses into the combination. Older adults should generally start at the low end and undergo slow titration with frequent breathing/CNS assessment and renal review. Frail or pulmonary-compromised patients may need a nonopioid alternative.

sources.sections: Drug Interactions / Pregnancy; Labor or Delivery; Boxed Warning

assertions: Human controlled data are insufficient; use only if potential benefit justifies fetal risk. Prolonged exposure can produce neonatal withdrawal requiring expert treatment. Placental transfer may cause neonatal respiratory depression; the combination is not recommended during or immediately before labor when other analgesic techniques are preferable.

sources.sections: Drug Interactions / Nursing Mothers; Infertility; Precautions / Lactation

assertions: Hydrocodone enters milk. Balance maternal need and breastfeeding benefits with infant risk; watch for unusual sleepiness, breathing difficulty or limpness and seek immediate care. Infant withdrawal can follow stopping maternal opioids or breastfeeding. The reviewed label does not establish breastfeeding safety or a universal safe dose. Extended opioid use may impair fertility, with reversibility uncertain.

Hydrocodone is a full opioid agonist with relative mu-receptor selectivity. It reduces pain perception but also suppresses brainstem respiratory responses, decreases gut motility and can lower blood pressure. APAP’s analgesic mechanism is incompletely established and thought to involve central actions; it does not prevent opioid sedation or dependence.

In a small labeled oral study, hydrocodone peaked around 1.3 hours with a half-life around 3.8 hours. CYP3A4 forms norhydrocodone; CYP2D6 forms hydromorphone. Hydrocodone/metabolites are mainly renally eliminated. APAP undergoes hepatic conjugation and a smaller oxidative pathway producing a reactive intermediate normally detoxified by glutathione; metabolites are excreted renally. APAP’s half-life is about 1.25–3 hours and may lengthen with liver damage or overdose.

sources.sections: Warnings; Precautions / Information for Patients; Dosage and Administration

assertions: Review pain/function benefit, sedation, respiratory rate, constipation, blood pressure, organ function, other drugs and misuse risk. Discuss dependence versus addiction and a planned stop/taper. Avoid driving until the individual response is known; do not share medication, self-increase doses or add alcohol/APAP products. Read the Medication Guide with each dispensing and plan bowel care.

Call emergency services for slow breathing, severe sleepiness or inability to wake; give the available reversal agent according to its own instructions and continue emergency care because recurrence is possible. Opioid reversal does not treat APAP poisoning. Suspected excess APAP needs urgent poison-center/emergency assessment even when the person feels well; clinicians assess timing, APAP levels and need for N-acetylcysteine. Do not wait for jaundice or other delayed liver signs.

sources.sections: Precautions / Storage and Disposal; Reversal Agent Access; Medication Guide

assertions: Keep locked or otherwise secure from children, visitors and diversion. Prefer a drug take-back option; the reviewed Medication Guide directs prompt flushing of unwanted tablets when take-back is not readily available. Make sure household members know where the reversal medicine is and how to obtain emergency help.

Reviewed Strides 5 mg/325 mg tablets are white and capsule-shaped, marked P on one side and 36 04 on the other. The Proficient Rx bottle of 12 has NDC 82804-306-12 and source NDC 64380-440. Other manufacturers or strengths can look different.

sources.sections: Description; Dosage and Administration; How Supplied

assertions: The reviewed oral immediate-release tablet label describes hydrocodone bitartrate/APAP 5/325, 7.5/325 and 10/325 mg. The representative repackaging is only 5/325. Liquid, extended-release and other combination products require their own labels; do not infer dose equivalence from this page.

sources.sections: How Supplied; Precautions / Storage and Disposal

assertions: Store the reviewed tablets at 20–25°C in a tight, light-resistant container with a child-resistant closure. Keep securely out of sight and reach of children; child-resistant packaging alone does not prevent accidental ingestion. Follow the actual package’s instructions.

validationEvidence.caveat: Local checks and representative visual inspection passed; production deployment pending.

sources.title: Zepbound · Current prescribing information
sources.note: PI revised August 2026; SPL40 effective August 28, published September 2, 2026. Adult weight-management and OSA; single/multidose devices.
sources.review_method: Full relevant clinical SPL sections read; dosing/product table text checked against the source; current manufacturer PDF concordance checked for tirzepatide.
sources.access: Full substantive clinical sections/SPL IFUs read; current 33-page manufacturer PDF opened and cross-checked

assertions: Mounjaro complements diet/exercise for glycemic control in type 2 diabetes in adults and children age 10 years or older. The current August 2026 label also approves reducing major adverse cardiovascular events—CV death, nonfatal MI or nonfatal stroke—in adults with type 2 diabetes at high risk for those events. This adult CV indication does not establish pediatric CV prevention.

With reduced-calorie nutrition and increased activity, Zepbound reduces excess weight and maintains weight reduction in adults with obesity, or overweight plus at least one weight-related comorbidity. It also treats moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea in adults with obesity. Pediatric effectiveness is not established; the current label does not give a separate CV, kidney-outcome or MASH indication.

Zepbound coadministration with another tirzepatide product or any GLP-1 agonist is not recommended. Use one product and a coordinated treatment plan; these labels do not authorize type 1-diabetes treatment. Mounjaro’s adult cardiovascular trial established noninferiority to dulaglutide, not superiority, so its new indication should not be presented as superiority evidence.

The current label starts at 2.5 mg subcutaneously weekly. If additional glycemic control is needed, increase in 2.5 mg steps after at least 4 weeks at the current dose. Maximum: adults 15 mg/week; pediatric patients age 10 years or older, 10 mg/week. Unlike Zepbound, this revision no longer states that 2.5 mg must be increased to 5 mg after 4 weeks or is nontherapeutic. The current label does not specify a separate fixed dose solely for cardiovascular-risk reduction.

Start 2.5 mg subcutaneously weekly for 4 weeks, then increase to 5 mg weekly. Further 2.5 mg steps require at least 4 weeks at each dose; select by response and tolerability. The 2.5 mg dose is for initiation, not maintenance.

For either brand, give a missed dose within 96 hours; otherwise skip and resume the usual weekly day. Changing the weekday requires at least 72 hours between doses. Inject at any time, with or without meals, into abdomen or thigh; another person can inject the back of the upper arm. Rotate sites. Mounjaro and insulin must be separate injections, never mixed, and not adjacent.

Single-dose pens/vials deliver 0.5 mL; multidose vials and KwikPens deliver 0.6 mL per weekly dose. A vial user needs an appropriate syringe, such as 1 mL with the required volume graduations, and a new syringe/needle each time. KwikPens contain four fixed weekly doses: use a new compatible needle, prime as instructed and dial the full prescribed dose; do not count clicks, withdraw pen contents into a syringe or inject leftover drug after four doses. Never share pens even after changing needles.

Training must match the prescribed presentation and be repeated after a device change. Mounjaro KwikPen is not recommended for pediatric self-administration; visually impaired users need trained help for either KwikPen. Do not interpret adult single-dose-device familiarity as competency with a multidose device.

Persistent or severe abdominal pain, with or without vomiting, can signal pancreatitis: stop tirzepatide and obtain assessment. Evaluate suspected gallbladder disease. Severe GI reactions occur; neither brand is recommended with severe gastroparesis. Persistent vomiting/diarrhea may cause dehydration and acute kidney injury; follow renal function particularly during initiation/escalation.

Insulin or secretagogues increase hypoglycemia risk; consider dose reduction and glucose monitoring. Zepbound can also cause hypoglycemia without diabetes. Rapid glucose improvement can worsen diabetic retinopathy temporarily; monitor pre-existing retinopathy and report vision changes.

Rare pulmonary aspiration has occurred despite fasting during anesthesia/deep sedation. Tell the procedural team about treatment; the labels do not establish a universal preoperative hold interval. Never share a KwikPen. Evaluate serious allergy urgently and discontinue.

Both brands are contraindicated with personal or family medullary thyroid carcinoma, MEN2, or prior serious hypersensitivity to tirzepatide or the product’s excipients. Anaphylaxis and angioedema have been reported. Severe gastroparesis is a not-recommended warning, not an additional labeled formal contraindication.

Tirzepatide caused C-cell tumors in rats at clinically relevant exposures; whether it causes human MTC is unknown. Counsel about neck masses, persistent hoarseness and swallowing/breathing difficulty. Routine calcitonin screening or thyroid ultrasound has uncertain value; discovered nodules or elevated calcitonin require evaluation. This warning concerns MTC/MEN2, not a claim that all thyroid disease is contraindicated.

Common Mounjaro reactions include nausea, diarrhea, appetite reduction, vomiting, constipation, dyspepsia and abdominal pain. Zepbound also commonly reports injection reactions, fatigue, hypersensitivity, belching, hair loss and reflux. Pediatric Mounjaro patients had more vomiting, abdominal pain and hypoglycemia than adults. Postmarketing reports include pancreatitis, ileus/obstruction, severe constipation, serious allergy, aspiration and renal injury; spontaneous reports cannot establish incidence.

Switch to a nonoral contraceptive method or add barrier contraception for 4 weeks after starting tirzepatide and for 4 weeks after each dose escalation. Nonoral hormonal contraceptives should not be affected by gastric-emptying changes. This instruction applies to both brands.

Monitor oral drugs needing a threshold concentration or a narrow therapeutic range, such as warfarin, because absorption can change. Consider reducing insulin or secretagogues at initiation and follow glucose/hypoglycemia symptoms. Avoid assuming a low CYP interaction potential means no clinically relevant interactions.

Neither label recommends dose adjustment for renal impairment, including ESRD, or hepatic impairment because PK was not meaningfully changed. Monitor renal function when severe GI symptoms or volume depletion occur, especially during escalation. This PK finding does not establish a kidney-disease treatment indication.

Mounjaro diabetes approval begins at 10 years, with a 10 mg weekly maximum; younger-child safety/effectiveness is not established. Zepbound pediatric safety/effectiveness is not established. Older-adult trials generally found no overall difference, but Zepbound OSA trials had too few age 65+ participants for a firm age comparison. Consider frailty, intake and tolerability individually.

Human pregnancy evidence is insufficient and animal findings raise fetal concern. Mounjaro use requires benefit-risk assessment alongside the risks of uncontrolled maternal diabetes. Zepbound should be discontinued when pregnancy is recognized because weight loss has no pregnancy benefit and may harm the fetus. Discuss pregnancy plans and alternative therapy; do not import semaglutide’s two-month washout as a tirzepatide label instruction. Follow the contraception precautions above.

Current labels report a single 5 mg study in 11 lactating adults: most milk samples were undetectable, and total detected drug was below 0.02% of the administered maternal dose. This is not evidence of steady-state infant safety; effects on infants and milk production remain unknown. Balance maternal need, breastfeeding benefits and potential infant risk rather than declaring breastfeeding universally safe or contraindicated.

Tirzepatide activates GIP and GLP-1 receptors, promotes glucose-dependent insulin secretion, reduces glucagon and improves insulin sensitivity. Appetite/calorie-intake effects reduce weight. Delayed gastric emptying is greatest after the first dose and diminishes with repeated treatment, explaining oral-absorption precautions.

After subcutaneous dosing, bioavailability is about 80%, peak concentrations occur 8–72 hours later and steady state is reached after about 4 weeks. Albumin binding is about 99%. The Mounjaro label gives an approximately 5-day half-life; Zepbound reports about 5–6 days in obesity/OSA populations. Proteolysis, fatty-acid beta-oxidation and amide hydrolysis form metabolites excreted in urine and feces; intact drug is not detected in those routes.

Follow glucose and A1c for diabetes, weight/tolerability for weight management, and the OSA plan and symptoms for sleep-apnea treatment. Maintain clinical management of cardiovascular risk alongside Mounjaro. Review hydration, renal symptoms, abdominal pain, visual changes and hypoglycemia; reassess interacting oral medicines and contraceptive protection. Routine thyroid screening solely because of tirzepatide has uncertain value.

Use the prescribed weekly milligram dose and presentation-specific IFU. Do not improvise pen clicks or leftover doses; dispose of needles in a sharps container. Report severe persistent GI symptoms, dehydration, vision changes, a neck mass or serious allergy. Tell anesthesia clinicians before procedures. Suspected overdose needs poison-center/medical advice and supportive care; the long half-life may require extended observation.

Lilly Mounjaro 2.5 mg/0.5 mL single-dose pens: carton of 4, NDC 0002-1506-80. Lilly Zepbound 2.5 mg/0.5 mL single-dose pens: carton of 4, NDC 0002-2506-80. These are examples, not a list of every package. Check the actual brand, dose and device.

Both current labels list single-dose pens/vials, multidose vials and single-patient-use KwikPens at 2.5, 5, 7.5, 10, 12.5 or 15 mg per weekly dose. Single-dose products use 0.5 mL; multidose products deliver four 0.6 mL doses from 2.4 mL. KwikPen contains priming allowance; total content is not one injection. Multidose contents are shown below.

Protect from heat/light in the original carton; do not freeze or use a frozen product. Refrigerate unopened products at 2–8°C. Single-dose pens/vials can spend a total of 21 days at ≤30°C, then must be discarded; discard an opened single-dose vial after use.

Unopened multidose vials/KwikPens can remain refrigerated to expiry, but must be discarded after 30 days at room temperature ≤30°C. For an opened multidose product, section 16.2 permits refrigeration or room temperature; discard at the earliest of 30 total room-temperature days, 30 days after first use, or four weekly doses, even with medicine remaining.

The device IFU should also be followed: a KwikPen needs its cap, no attached needle during storage, priming before each dose and no attempted extraction of leftover drug. Presentation-specific guidance supersedes any assumption that all pens have the 21-day single-dose rule.

validationEvidence.caveat: Local checks and representative visual inspection passed; production deployment pending.

assertions: Ritalin immediate-release tablets are labeled for ADHD in children age 6 and older and adults, and for narcolepsy. Concerta is labeled for ADHD at ages 6–65. Ritalin LA’s current label restricts its ADHD indication to ages 6–12. Quillivant XR is labeled for ADHD with dosing from age 6; it is not recommended below age 6.

This profile covers these four oral products. Daytrana patches, other delayed/extended-release tablets or capsules, chewables, and other liquids require their own administration and conversion instructions. Do not extend the immediate-release narcolepsy indication to the selected ADHD-only extended-release labels.

Age ≥6: start 5 mg twice daily before breakfast and lunch; increase by 5–10 mg per week. Doses above 60 mg/day are not recommended. Adults: the label describes an average total dose of 20–30 mg/day in two or three divided doses, preferably 30–45 minutes before meals; maximum 60 mg/day. If late dosing causes insomnia, take the last dose before 6 p.m. The adult average is not a mandatory starting dose.
Take once each morning with or without food. Increase in 18-mg steps at weekly intervals; 27 mg permits a smaller increase from 18 mg. Swallow tablets whole with liquid; do not split, crush, or chew.
Age 6–12 | 18 mg daily / 18–54 mg daily
Age 13–17 | 18 mg daily / 18–72 mg daily, not above 2 mg/kg/day
Age 18–65 | 18 or 36 mg daily / 18–72 mg daily

For its labeled age 6–12 population, start 20 mg each morning, or 10 mg when a lower start is appropriate; increase by 10 mg weekly. Above 60 mg/day is not recommended. Swallow whole, or sprinkle the entire bead contents on a spoonful of non-warm applesauce and consume immediately. Never chew, crush, divide, or store the mixture.

Age ≥6: start 20 mg each morning; increase weekly by 10–20 mg. Above 60 mg/day is unstudied and not recommended. After pharmacist reconstitution the concentration is 25 mg/5 mL (5 mg/mL); 20 mg is 4 mL. Shake vigorously for at least 10 seconds before every dose and measure with the supplied oral dispenser. Take with or without food. Patients must not reconstitute the powder themselves.

Concerta has a specific table for prior immediate-release doses taken twice or three times daily: 5 mg/dose → 18 mg each morning; 10 → 36; 15 → 54; 20 → 72, with the 72-mg conversion limited to ages 13–65. Ritalin LA has a separate twice-daily Ritalin conversion table; other products require discontinuation and product-specific titration. Quillivant XR explicitly requires retitration rather than a milligram-for-milligram swap. Respect each age maximum. Reduce or discontinue for paradoxical worsening/adverse effects; the labels advise discontinuation if no improvement after appropriate adjustment over one month.

Avoid use with serious structural heart disease, cardiomyopathy, serious arrhythmias, coronary disease, or other serious cardiac disease. Monitor blood pressure and pulse. Screen for manic risk and assess new psychosis or mania; review new/worsening tics or Tourette symptoms. Watch growth, weight, appetite, peripheral circulation changes, and digital sores. Persistent painful erections require immediate care, including during withdrawal or drug holidays.

Evaluate glaucoma risk: acute angle-closure reports and increased intraocular pressure warrant ophthalmic assessment and monitoring when indicated. Concerta’s nondeformable tablet is generally inappropriate with severe GI narrowing and must be swallowable whole. Current ER labels/FDA warn that children under 6 have higher exposure and adverse-event risks, including weight loss; no preschool ER regimen is supplied.

All four labels contraindicate hypersensitivity to methylphenidate/product ingredients and concurrent MAO inhibitors or use within 14 days after stopping an MAOI. Serious cardiac disease, tics, and glaucoma are addressed under current warnings, rather than being added to these formal contraindication lists.

sourceAudit.card_title: Boxed warning: abuse, misuse, and addiction
assertions: Methylphenidate has substantial abuse and misuse potential that can progress to addiction. Overdose and death are possible, especially with excessive doses or unapproved routes. Assess risk before prescribing, teach secure storage and disposal, and reassess for misuse throughout treatment. These products are U.S. Schedule II controlled substances.

Appetite loss, insomnia, anxiety, headache, abdominal discomfort, nausea, tachycardia, and weight loss are reported; frequency depends on product and population. Serious allergic, cardiovascular, neurologic, vascular, and ocular events also occur. Overdose can cause arrhythmias, severe blood-pressure disturbance, agitation, seizures, serotonin syndrome, hyperthermia, and rhabdomyolysis. Obtain emergency/poison-center help and account for delayed release; dialysis is not useful.

The MAOI combination and 14-day interval are contraindicated because of hypertensive crisis risk. Stimulants may reduce antihypertensive effectiveness; monitor blood pressure and adjust that therapy if needed. Halogenated anesthetics can cause abrupt blood-pressure/pulse increases; labels direct avoiding stimulant use on the day of surgery with those agents.

Changing either methylphenidate or risperidone dose during combined use can increase extrapyramidal symptoms; monitor movements. Ritalin LA and Quillivant XR direct avoiding alcohol because their release profiles may change; do not generalize this release effect to Concerta. Serotonin syndrome has been reported with methylphenidate plus serotonergic drugs, warranting medication review and assessment of concerning symptoms.

Pregnancy wording differs: Ritalin/Ritalin LA report no identified drug-associated risk in available reports, Concerta describes inconsistent findings, and Quillivant XR calls data insufficient. None proves absence of risk; consider treatment need, fetal perfusion concerns, and the pregnancy registry. Labels describe low milk exposure but unknown long-term infant neurodevelopment; monitor agitation, sleep, feeding, and weight. LactMed considers medically needed methylphenidate compatible with continuing breastfeeding on limited evidence, while warning that high doses may reduce milk production.

Use the product’s approved ages. ER products are not recommended below age 6; monitor height and weight, with interruption considered if expected growth fails. Concerta is not indicated above age 65; Ritalin, Ritalin LA, and Quillivant XR lack geriatric study evidence. No unsupported older-adult regimen is provided.

Formal organ-impairment evidence is limited. Ritalin/Ritalin LA expect little effect because metabolism is largely ester hydrolysis and little unchanged drug is renally cleared, but those populations were not studied. Concerta supplies no renal/hepatic PK information; Quillivant XR has no clinical experience in these populations. No validated numeric adjustment is invented.

Methylphenidate inhibits dopamine and norepinephrine reuptake; the precise therapeutic mechanism in ADHD/narcolepsy is not established. The racemate contains a more pharmacologically active d-enantiomer.

Ester hydrolysis forms largely inactive ritalinic acid, subsequently excreted mainly in urine. IR Ritalin peaks around 2 hours; Concerta has an early rise then prolonged delivery, typically peaking at 6–10 hours. Ritalin LA has two release phases; Quillivant XR’s fasting median peak in its adult study was about 5 hours. These product-specific data do not establish a universal conversion or equivalent duration.

Before treatment obtain cardiac history, family history of sudden death/arrhythmia, and examination; assess tics, manic risk, and misuse risk. Follow pulse, blood pressure, growth/weight, appetite, sleep, psychiatric symptoms, circulation, and goal-specific treatment response. Reassess adherence, interactions, and formulation before escalating.

Do not share or use unapproved routes. Keep medicine securely locked when possible and use approved disposal/take-back options. Teach the specific swallow/sprinkle/shake instructions. Concerta’s intact-looking shell may appear in stool after drug release. Seek urgent help for chest pain, fainting, severe psychosis, painful prolonged erection, eye pain/vision changes, or severe allergic symptoms.

Ritalin 5-mg tablets are round yellow, marked CIBA 7 (100-count NDC 66758-273-01). Concerta 18-mg tablets are yellow, marked alza 18 (100-count NDC 50458-585-01). Ritalin LA 10-mg capsules are white/light brown, marked NVR R10 (100-count NDC 0078-0424-05). Quillivant XR is a beige-to-tan suspension after reconstitution; its 60-mL package is NDC 24478-321-02. These identities refer to the cited manufacturers.

Selected products: Ritalin IR tablets 5/10/20 mg; Concerta ER tablets 18/27/36/54 mg; Ritalin LA ER capsules 10/20/30/40 mg; Quillivant XR reconstituted ER suspension 25 mg/5 mL, final bottle volumes 60/120/150/180 mL. A larger total dose can require multiple units; strengths of other brands are outside this scope.

Ritalin/Ritalin LA: 20–25°C with 15–30°C excursions; Ritalin needs light protection in a tight, light-resistant container and LA a tight container. Concerta: 25°C with 15–30°C excursions, protect from humidity. Quillivant XR: 25°C with 15–30°C excursions, original bottle/carton with adapter and dispenser; stable up to 4 months after pharmacist reconstitution. Secure all products against access and diversion.
